item.title: How a Room Gets a Year Attached to It
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The dining chairs do not match the table, and that is the first honest thing in the house. The table is oak, heavy, a little thirsty on top where someone once used it as a desk. The chairs are metal, black, the kind a catalog called “industrial” in 2014 and a thrift store now calls “chairs.” Between them sits a decade. You can feel it in the way guests pick a seat: they trust the table and they test the chairs. Furniture fashion is that interval — the time between a purchase that was trying to say something and a leftover that only has to hold a body.

Taste cycles in rooms the way hemlines cycle in photographs, only slower and more expensive to undo. A sofa is not a dress. You cannot bag it up in May. You live with last year’s certainty while this year’s catalog trains your eye to see it as a mistake. That lag is the business. Retail needs the lag. If last year’s sectional still looked finished, this year’s sectional would be optional.

Photo cue: FFF-01a — Two objects in one frame: a worn solid-oak dining table and a set of 2010s black metal “industrial” chairs; no lifestyle hands, daylight, scuffs visible.

Status is the second clock. A room is a claim about the person who paid for it. Mid-century modern, when it was new, claimed the future: Charles and Ray Eames’s lounge for Herman Miller in 1956, Florence Knoll’s corporate calm, the idea that a house could look like an airport lounge and that this was a compliment. Mediterranean oak in 1972 claimed Old World substance — carved, dark, Spanish by way of North Carolina. Black lacquer and brass in 1986 claimed money that had somewhere to be by eight. Distressed white in 1997 claimed inherited ease you had in fact bought at a boutique in Santa Monica. A barn door in 2015 claimed rural authenticity in a house that had never seen a barn. Quiet oak and linen in 2023 claimed that you had stopped claiming things. Each claim was sincere in its year. Sincerity does not prevent a year from ending.

The American furniture trade has always needed a picture before it needed a chair. The 1923 Sears catalog sold rooms as finished thoughts; you could point at a page and become that page. Ethan Allen later sold the same idea with a designer who came to the house. Design Within Reach, which Rob Forbes started in 1999 after failing to furnish a San Francisco apartment without a trade handshake, sold designer biographies next to the objects and made modernism feel like literacy. IKEA’s catalog, arriving in American mailboxes after the Plymouth Meeting, Pennsylvania, store opened on June 12, 1985, sold a whole apartment as a readable story in flat color. Instagram sold the story without the paper. The object is late to its own fashion. The picture is early.

High Point, North Carolina, still gathers the wholesale version of this twice a year. Buyers walk temporary rooms and decide what a sofa arm will be in the stores that have not yet been told. Thomasville, Lexington, Broyhill — the old factory names — taught the country that a style could be a line, a line could be a suite, and a suite could be a truck. Fashion in furniture is not a lone genius in Milan, though Milan has had those (Ettore Sottsass’s Memphis group opened at Arc ’74 in September 1981, fifty-five objects, and the argument is still loud). Fashion in furniture is also a buyer from a regional chain writing a number on a pad in a showroom that will be plywood again on Monday.

Photo cue: FFF-01b — High Point Market showroom corridor or a period trade-ad page for a named manufacturer suite; museum or trade-archive rights.

What ages and what dates is not a mystery if you stay in the material. A finish that belongs to the wood — oil, shellac, a stain that does not pretend to be another species — can be ugly for a decade and handsome again when the ugly decade ends. A finish that is the decade (harvest gold plastic, printed oak on particleboard, a gray-wash that exists to match Agreeable Gray) has nowhere to go when the decade leaves. Upholstery is almost always fashion. That is not an insult. Fabric takes a body and a sunbeam and a spill; it is supposed to be replaceable. The crime is a frame that cannot take a second fabric, or a cushion that was never a cushion so much as a first impression.

Particleboard is the twentieth century’s honest cheapness and its most common lie. Max Himmelheber’s German work in the 1930s made a useful board from waste and necessity [CITE NEEDED: patent number and year, often given as 1932 or 1933]. IKEA made that board a philosophy: furniture for the many, flat in a box, cheap enough to leave behind. The lie is the paper photograph of oak glued to the board, edged in plastic the color of oak, sold as wood to a person who wanted wood. Solid hardwood is not a moral victory. It is a mechanical one. You can plane it. You can glue a broken leg. You can hate the stain and change it. Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, prints “no particleboard” on its own product copy and dates a lumber ancestor, Bradley Lumber Co., to 1902; treat that date as company copy until a primary record sits beside it [CITE NEEDED]. The useful contrast is not heritage theater. It is a top you can sand after the fashion color fails.

People buy fads because rooms have to be lived in now. A first apartment needs a table before it needs an heirloom. A young family needs a sofa that can take juice. A retired couple wants the living room to look decided before the grandchildren come. Fashion is how those needs get a shape in a given year. The Mediterranean dining set was a real table. The Cloud-style sectional, launched by RH in 2015 after Timothy Oulton’s long development with the company, is a real place to lie down. Rachel Ashwell’s slipcovered sofas, sold from Santa Monica after she opened Shabby Chic in 1989, were washable, which is a virtue. Chip and Joanna Gaines’s Fixer Upper (HGTV, 2013–2018) gave a lot of people permission to paint something white and feel they had begun. None of that deserves a sneer. What deserves a hard look is the object that was built to photograph and not to be repaired.

Photo cue: FFF-01c — A 1970s manufacturer brochure page (Thomasville, Broyhill, or Lane) showing a complete matching room; public collection or licensed ad archive.

The hangover is the part magazines skip because it is not pretty. It is the entertainment wall unit sized for a 32-inch television, too good to trash, too ugly to keep, occupying a basement in Fort Wayne. It is the barn door on a pantry in a 2017 spec house, off the track, leaning. It is the blush velvet chair listed online as “mid-century” by a seller who means 2017. It is the waterbed frame, Charles Hall’s late-1960s idea gone retail, now a curious rectangle in a garage [CITE NEEDED on Hall’s thesis year]. Hangovers are proof the fashion worked. If nobody had believed it, there would be nothing to trip over.

A hardwood shop that does not issue a color of the year is not above this system. It is beside it. The shop still has to sell. It still stains cherry darker when the market wants dark, lighter when the market wants pale. The difference is that the board remains a board. When the stain year ends, a person with sandpaper and patience can recover a table. When the board is a photograph, patience has nothing to hold.

This series is a walk through the rooms America was sold, decade by decade and object by object: the mid-century boom and the copies that ate it; the dark oak Spanish of the 1970s; lacquer and brass; shabby white; farmhouse iron; the quiet-luxury voice that arrived to scold the cart; the sofa that became architecture; the patio that became a second living room; the word “biophilic” printed on a cane headboard. It is also a walk through the shops that declined to look up from the joint — Gustav Stickley’s Craftsman (1901–1916), Thos. Moser’s Continuous Arm of 1977, the quieter American hardwood floors that never learned the word “collection launch.”

You do not have to pick a tribe. You can own a fashionable lamp and a boring table and be right about both. The only test worth keeping is simple, and it is not a vibe. Will this object still be itself when the picture that sold it is embarrassing? If yes, it is furniture. If no, it was a year. Years are allowed. Just know which you are buying, and what it will cost to stop living in it.

item.title: Mid-Century Boom and Hangover
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The rosewood is almost certainly not rosewood. You can tell from the door, before you sit, because the grain repeats every eighteen inches the way a printed ribbon repeats. The leather is a leather-like. The ottoman is a cube of foam with button tufts that were glued, not pulled. The listing says “Eames style,” which is the most American phrase in furniture: a name that once meant a factory in Michigan and a pair of designers in California, now a silhouette you can order by Friday.

Charles and Ray Eames’s lounge chair and ottoman left Herman Miller in 1956 as a serious object — molded plywood shells, a metal spine, leather that was meant to take a life. It was never cheap. It was never supposed to be the whole room. The hangover is that it became the room’s password. If you had the chair, or something that read as the chair from across a loft, you had joined a church that started as a factory and ended as a feed.

Photo cue: FFF-02a — Herman Miller Eames lounge, 1956 or later authorized production; object shot, rosewood or walnut clearly wood, not lifestyle. Rights: Herman Miller / Vitra archive license, or museum collection (MoMA, etc.).

Mid-century modern, as a living style, was not a single year. It was a twenty-year argument after the war: George Nelson at Herman Miller, Florence Knoll and Eero Saarinen at Knoll, the Danish export wave (Hans Wegner’s Round Chair, often called The Chair; Finn Juhl; Arne Jacobsen’s Series 7 for Fritz Hansen). American suburbs took a thinner version — blonde suites from Bassett and Lane, a kidney coffee table, a starburst clock — and called it modern because the legs were tapered. Both versions were sincere. The factory in Zeeland, Michigan, and the factory in Virginia were not doing the same work. They were answering the same wish: a house that did not look like grandmother’s mahogany.

The first hangover happened on schedule. By the mid-1970s, modern looked cold to a country that had just bought Mediterranean oak and harvest gold. The Eames chair did not disappear; it went into offices and the houses of people who had never believed the oak. Everyone else bought a carved suite and put a macramé owl on the wall. That is not a fall from grace. That is a cycle. The chair waited.

The boom that people mean when they say “mid-century is back” started as a retail education project. Rob Forbes founded Design Within Reach in 1999 (the idea, he has said, came in 1998 when he tried to furnish an apartment with the London modern he could not get through an American trade gate). The first catalogs put designer biographies next to SKUs. Herman Miller, which had not been a mall brand, sold through DWR’s paper and then its stores. The Washington Post noticed the catalog-to-store move in 2004. Herman Miller bought DWR in 2015, which is a tidy ending for a story about access: the factory absorbed the shop that had taught people to want the factory.

Dwell arrived on newsstands in October 2000, Lara Hedberg Deam’s magazine, Karrie Jacobs’s “Fruit Bowl Manifesto” insisting that modern houses were lived in, fruit on the table, not airless. The magazine did not invent the revival. It gave the revival a kitchen. Then Mad Men (AMC, 2007–2015) gave it a whiskey and a sofa people could point at without saying “Saarinen.” Television is a more efficient catalog than a catalog. You do not have to admit you are shopping.

Photo cue: FFF-02b — Dwell, October 2000, cover or “Fruit Bowl Manifesto” spread; fair-use thumbnail in an editor’s file, or US Modernist’s scan for research, rights before publish.

What the boom sold, after a while, was not the chair. It was the password. West Elm, launched by Williams-Sonoma in 2002, put tapered legs on prices a first apartment could stand. Article, AllModern, Wayfair’s modern filters, the “mid-century walnut” finish that was a photograph of walnut — these made a silhouette into a default. The status claim changed. In 1962 the Eames lounge said you knew architects. In 2012 the knockoff said you watched the right show and you were not your parents’ Tuscan kitchen. Same silhouette, different boast.

I will not pretend authorized production is innocent. Herman Miller and Vitra have spent decades policing a shape. Licensed chairs are still expensive because the name is the product as much as the shell. A person who buys the licensed chair is buying a factory’s continuity and a lawyer’s file. A person who buys the $79 version is buying a picture. Both are allowed. Only one will still be a chair when the picture is tired.

The hangover now is not that modern looks dated. Parts of it refuse to date, which is the problem. A Wegner wishbone — the CH24, Carl Hansen & Søn, from 1949 — still looks like a chair because it was a chair: steam-bent back, paper cord, a joint you can read. The hangover is the apartment in which every object is a wishbone’s cousin, in a walnut print, under a replica Sputnik, above a rug that is a copy of a copy of a David Hicks. The room does not look like 1956. It looks like 2014, which is a year that already has a flea-market section.

Danish teak of the 1950s and 1960s is the other boom, and it has a cleaner hangover because the originals were so often better than the copies. Real teak oilers know the weight. The copies are rubberwood or something called “teak finish.” Estate-sale prices for a Finn Juhl-attributed piece and a dining set that is only brown have split so far apart that the word “Danish” in a listing is now a test of the seller, not the object. Chairish and 1stDibs made that split a market. Craigslist still hides the sleeper that a person who knows joints can find.

Photo cue: FFF-02c — 1960s Danish teak dining table, oil finish, extension leaf; object, no staged family. Museum or dealer photo with rights; or a catalog page from a period importer (Georg Jensen, etc.).

What ages, in this story, is almost insultingly simple. Molded plywood that is actually plywood. A metal base with a real weld. Leather that can be conditioned and, later, replaced. A teak table whose top is teak through the thickness. What dates is the password used as wallpaper: the word “Eames” on a box that contains none of his decisions, the hairpin legs on a particleboard desk, the sunburst clock that was already a joke in 1998 and became sincere again in 2011 and is a joke again if you wait.

Retail did one more thing to the boom: it taught a generation that “authentic” was a SKU. Design Within Reach sold authorized pieces and also sold the idea that you were now the kind of person who knew the difference. The stores — glass, pale oak floors, a lounge on a plinth — were classrooms with price tags. You left knowing the name of a designer you had not known at lunch. That is not a small public service. It is also how a silhouette becomes homework. Once the homework is widely assigned, the knockoff is the crib sheet.

Knoll and Herman Miller had always sold to architects first. The revival sold to people who wanted to live as if an architect had already been there. The difference shows up in the accessories. A 1961 office with a Saarinen pedestal table did not need a replica Noguchi lamp from a site that also sells phone cases. A 2016 apartment often did, because the password had become a set, and sets are how fashion closes. Florence Knoll’s own interiors were spare because the furniture was the decision. The hangover interiors are crowded because the furniture is the costume.

Photo cue: FFF-02d — A Design Within Reach catalog spread, early 2000s, designer biography beside an authorized Herman Miller piece; catalog archive, rights before publish.

A hardwood shop watching this boom has a peculiar job. It cannot out-Eames Eames. It should not try. The useful thing it can do is refuse the printed grain that lets a “walnut credenza” exist at a price that walnut cannot. Bradley Brand’s own copy, out of Warren, Arkansas, insists on solid hardwood and no particleboard, and dates Bradley Lumber Co. to 1902 [CITE NEEDED — company copy]. That is not mid-century, and should not be sold as mid-century. It is a different bet: an object that does not need a designer biography because the board is the biography.

The Eameses were interested in how people sit and how factories might serve that sitting. The knockoff is interested in how people post. Both objects occupy the same corner of the room. Only one of them was designed for the corner. The other was designed for the frame. If you want the password, buy it cheap and admit the year. If you want the chair, buy the chair, or buy something else entirely that was also built to be sat in — a Windsor, a Continuous Arm, a kitchen chair with a seat you can recane. The hangover is full of passwords. It is short on chairs that were only chairs.

item.title: Mediterranean Oak, High Point Spanish
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The gentleman’s chest is too wide for the hallway, which is how you know it was never meant to live here. It is oak, or wants to be read as oak: a heavy brown that goes orange when the afternoon hits the raised drawer fronts, brass pulls with a blackened wash in the recesses, a carved arch over the upper doors that looks like a church window drawn from memory. Someone has stacked winter coats on the left side and a sewing machine on the right. The chest was sold as a bedroom, in a suite, with a triple dresser and a headboard that repeated the same arch. It is in a hallway now because the bedroom went gray and this piece would not.

Photo cue: FFF-03a — Thomasville Segovia gentleman’s chest or triple dresser, raised fronts, brass hardware, orange-brown oak; object shot, no staged couple. Rights: dealer photo with permission, or a period manufacturer brochure if licensed.

This was American factory Spanish, and it had a name. Thomasville Furniture, working out of Thomasville and showing in High Point, North Carolina, put the Segovia collection on bedroom floors in the years when a suite was still the unit of sale: dresser, chest, nightstands, bed, sometimes a bench. Segovia was the Spanish Mediterranean oak that a lot of the country meant when it said Mediterranean — distressed finish, brass hardware, raised door and drawer fronts, carving that read as Old World from the aisle. Dealer listings still call some of those cases solid oak and mention dovetails. Treat the listings as listings. A factory can claim a solid carcass and still print a costume on the doors.

Broyhill and a dozen other Carolina and Virginia names ran adjacent lines in the late 1960s and through the 1970s: Mediterranean, Spanish Colonial, a carved oak that was not a copy of one Spanish room so much as a mood assembled from catalogs. Dark dining rooms. Wrought-iron chandeliers with yellow glass. Doors with panels that wanted to be a hacienda. Red shag, or a rust sculptured carpet, running up to the base of a table that could have hosted a treaty. The adjacency mattered. The furniture did not invent the decade. It sat in a decade that had already decided brown was substance and carving was history.

None of it was Mediterranean vernacular. A farm table from Catalonia or a painted chest from a Greek island does not look like a 1973 bedroom suite from High Point. The American version was a factory’s idea of Spain: arches, turned feet, a stain that made new oak look inherited. Inheritance, in those showrooms, was a finish. You could buy a past on a Saturday and have it delivered before the in-laws came. That is not a crime. It is a retail service. The country had just finished a long run of blonde modern and walnut dingbat, and it wanted weight.

Status, then, was Old World without a passport. A Segovia bedroom said you had arrived at a kind of adulthood that mid-century had not offered: dark, carved, complete. The gentleman’s chest — a tall case with doors over drawers, sold as the man’s piece in a matched pair — was the boast inside the suite. It held suits, or it was supposed to. A lot of them held Christmas wrap and a bowling bag. The triple dresser held the rest of a marriage’s hardware: jewelry trays, a church bulletin, a comb. Formal dining under the same stain said the same sentence in a louder room. You were not the family with the kidney coffee table anymore. You were the family with a sideboard.

High Point taught the trade that a style could be a line and a line could fill a truck. Buyers walked temporary rooms and wrote numbers. Thomasville’s name on a hangtag was a kind of literacy; Broyhill’s price was a kind of permission. Department stores and the big regional floors — the Levitz boxes, the local galleries that smelled of stain and new carpet — sold the suite as a finished thought. You did not pick a chest. You picked a Spain. The Spain was made in North Carolina. That fact was not hidden. It was also not the point. The point was the arch.

Photo cue: FFF-03b — Period Thomasville or Broyhill Mediterranean brochure page, complete bedroom or dining suite; trade-ad archive or museum collection, rights before publish.

The dining rooms are the ones people remember with the most heat, because they ate in them. Dark oak table, two captain’s chairs with arms that bruised a hip, a hutch with glass doors and a plate groove. A wrought-iron light that rusted in the humidity and still hung. Red shag that collected gravy and a dog. Harvest gold in the kitchen next door, avocado if the appliances had been bought in the same binge. The dining set and the appliances were not one collection. They were one year wearing two departments. When the year ended, the appliances were easier to hate. The table was heavier.

What dates, in this story, is the costume and the stain as a calendar. The carved arch that repeats on every door of a suite is a year even when the oak is real. The orange-brown that catalogs called pecan or Mediterranean oak — a warm, slightly pumpkin dusk — is a year the way harvest gold is a year. You can live with it. You cannot pretend it is 1820. Raised moldings that exist to catch a highlight in a showroom photograph catch dust in a hallway. Distressed edges applied at the factory, a little too even, a little too kind, read as a product after twenty years of real knocks have added a second, less polite wear. Two times stacked. The later time is honest. The factory time is a drawing.

What ages is blunter. A solid oak case with drawers that are actually joined — some Segovia pieces, again, show dovetails in the listings, and a dovetail you can see is a dovetail you can trust more than a photograph of one — can take a new finish, a new pull, a life that is not a suite. The gentleman’s chest in the hallway is ugly in the present mood and still a chest. You can oil the top. You can replace the brass if the brass has gone the color of a forgotten key. You can leave the brass, which is often better. What you cannot do is sand a stamped panel back into a tree. If the door is a carving of a carving, pressed into a skin, the costume is the object.

I have seen Segovia-adjacent suites broken up at estate sales in towns that never used the word Segovia. The headboard goes first, because headboards are fashion. The nightstands go to a college apartment and get painted. The triple dresser waits. It is too useful to dump and too brown to photograph. Someone’s cousin takes it for a guest room. That is the hangover: not a crash, a diaspora. The matched Spain becomes four pieces in four houses, each of them slightly ashamed of the arch and grateful for the drawers.

The 1980s did not argue with this oak so much as walk into another room. Black lacquer, brass, a glass cocktail table, a pastel Southwestern that wanted sun instead of cathedral. Mediterranean oak went to the basement, then to the cabin, then to the resale barn where it sits under a fluorescent tube and looks heavier than the price. A later generation, trained by mid-century feeds, called it grandma oak and meant an insult. Some of it was printed grain and earned the insult. Some of it was a board. The insult did not sort them.

Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, does not sell a Spanish collection. The company’s own copy still points at hardwood, at no particleboard, and at a lumber ancestor, Bradley Lumber Co., dated 1902; treat that date as company copy until a primary record sits beside it [CITE NEEDED]. The useful contrast is not heritage theater and not a sermon about North Carolina factories. It is a case you can refinish when the orange-brown year is over. A carved-arch costume on a photograph of oak has nowhere to go except paint or the curb. A solid oak box with a joint you can get back into can wait out the mood. Waiting is not virtue. It is joinery.

The Mediterranean boom was a sincere wish. People wanted a dining room that felt older than the subdivision. They wanted a bedroom that did not look like a motel modern. High Point sold them a Spain that could be financed. The hangover is the chest in the hallway, still doing chest work, still wearing a church window that never saw a mass. You do not have to keep the arch. You can keep the drawers. If the drawers are oak through the thickness, you are not stuck with 1974. You are stuck with a piece of furniture, which is a better sentence.

A hardwood shop watching this cycle has one job that is not nostalgia. Refuse the printed grain that lets a “Spanish oak” exist at a price oak cannot. Let the carving be carving, or let it go. Do not distress a new edge to impersonate a century. If a customer wants dark, stain dark, and say it is stain. The Segovia rooms were not lying about wanting weight. They were lying, when they lied, about time. Time is the one finish a factory cannot spray.

Photo cue: FFF-03c — Estate-sale or thrift hallway: a Mediterranean oak chest used as a coat dump, red or rust carpet remnant if it survives; no mockery in the lighting.

item.title: Lacquer, Brass, and the Other Eighties
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The cocktail table is a rectangle of smoked glass on a brass X, and it still has a ring from a plant that was never emptied. Under the glass: a remote, a TV Guide from a year the magazine still existed, a book of matches from a restaurant that is now a parking lot. The dining room beyond it is black lacquer, or a black that wants to be lacquer — high shine, brass ferrules on the chair legs, a sideboard that reflects the chandelier as a smear. This is not Memphis. This is the American 1980s as a furniture floor sold them: power, gloss, metal that caught a downlight. Memphis was the argument in Milan. This table is what the argument looked like after it went through a catalog.

Photo cue: FFF-04a — Brass-and-glass cocktail table, smoked or clear, mall scale; black-lacquer dining fragment in the same room if possible. Object, fingerprints allowed. Rights: period interior or original still-life.

The Memphis group was constituted on December 11, 1980, in Ettore Sottsass’s apartment in Milan. The first collection showed at the Arc ’74 gallery during the Milan Furniture Fair in September 1981. Sources split on the opening day: the 18th or the 19th. Say both. Fifty-five pieces. Sottsass’s Carlton and Casablanca — the totem bookcases that look like a cartoon of a cabinet and a cabinet of a cartoon — and Martine Bedin’s Super Lamp, a snake of colored bulbs on wheels, were the images that left the room. Plastic laminate, cheap and shiny, used as if it were marble. Color that refused beige. Forms that refused the good taste the Italian factories had been exporting as modern.

Karl Lagerfeld furnished a Monte Carlo apartment in Memphis. Artnet, citing a 1983 German magazine interview, has him calling it “love at first sight” and “the Art Deco of the ’80s.” Quote it that way: through the citation, not as a line you overheard. Sottsass left the group in 1985. Memphis dissolved around 1988. Eight years, or a little less, depending on how you count the afterlife of the photographs. The photographs did better than the sofas. They still do.

American rooms did not, as a rule, buy a Carlton. They bought a parallel 1980s that shared a shine and refused the joke. Black lacquer dining suites. Brass-and-glass coffee tables from the mall and from the better galleries. Lane and Henredon in high gloss: dining and bedroom case goods that wanted to look wet. A Lane table from those years, if the finish is actually lacquer on a real top, still takes a light if you dust it. A mall cousin with a film on a hollow apron does not. Yuppie power rooms — the word is dated, the rooms were real — held a lacquer desk, a brass lamp, a leather chair that faced a city or a golf print, a blotter that never saw ink. The status claim was money that had somewhere to be by eight. You were not the Mediterranean-oak person. You were not waiting for Old World. You were already late.

The other 1980s sat in the next subdivision: Southwestern pastels, bleached pine, a howling coyote, terracotta that had never been clay. Same decade, opposite boast. One room said night and metal. One room said sun and dust. Both rooms were sold by the same kind of floor, sometimes on the same Saturday, to people who would not have recognized Sottsass’s name and did not need to. Fashion in furniture is allowed to fork. A buyer could walk out of a department store with a brass-and-glass table and, two weekends later, a washed-pine dinette for the sunroom, and feel consistent both times. The hangover is that both forks are now in the same thrift store, and only one of them still looks like a decision.

Memphis, for all its laminate, was an argument about taste. The American gloss suite was an argument about evening. The power room wanted to look like an office that had been invited home. High Point showed both the joke and the evening, and buyers wrote numbers on the evening. That is not a failure of Milan. Milan was never going to furnish Columbus. Columbus was going to furnish Columbus, with a shine it could finance.

Photo cue: FFF-04b — Memphis Carlton or Casablanca, museum or archive shot, laminate and color honest; or a 1981 press photograph from Arc ’74 if rights clear. Do not pass a replica as the 1981 piece.

Retail had a ladder here, as it always does. At the top: the actual Memphis objects, then the Italian and French names that used lacquer as a craft — a chest built to take a polish, edges that were edges. In the middle: Henredon, Lane, the department-store gloss suites, brass that was brass. At the bottom: the mall cocktail table, a hollow brass-colored tube, a glass that chipped at the corner, a dining set whose “lacquer” was a film on particleboard that telegraphed every hip check as a white moon. IKEA’s American life had started in 1985, in Plymouth Meeting, Pennsylvania, and it would eventually teach a different shine — birch, white, a price that did not require a power job. In the mid-1980s the mall table still felt like arrival.

What ages is a well-made lacquer chest. Lacquer, done as a finish and not as a sticker, can be cut back, built up, repaired by a finisher who still owns the word. The box underneath has to be a box: solid wood or a stable core with an honest skin, drawers that run, a top that is a plane. Black will go in and out of fashion the way black suits do. The chest does not have to apologize for 1986 if 1986 was a construction and not a costume. A brass pull that is brass can be cleaned. It can also stay dull. Dull brass on a good box is not a failure. It is a surface that has been touched.

What dates is the brass-and-glass cocktail table from the mall. The X-base, the glass that never sat quite level, the ferrules that loosened, the way every magazine and every remote lived in public because the table had no drawers and no shame. That table was a year even when it was new. It photographed as money. It lived as a dust farm. Southwestern pastel, in the other room, dated on a different clock — sun-struck pine going cheap, a coyote going joke — but the mall brass table dated as soon as the next catalog put a wood slab on hairpin legs and called it honest. Honesty is a fashion word. The table was never claiming honesty. It was claiming night.

The hangover is specific and still in storage units. A black dining set too formal for the way people eat now, which is at the island, standing. A mirrored dresser from a “contemporary” bedroom group, the mirrors foxed, the brass going the color of a forgotten hinge. A Memphis poster, or a Memphis-ish print, in a frame that was also brass. The real Carlton, when it appears at auction, is an artifact with a price that has nothing to do with a den in Columbus. The replica Carlton, sold later as a silhouette, is a password, the way the Eames knockoff is a password. Same problem, louder colors.

I will not sneer at the buyer who wanted the shine. A first good job, a first dining room that was not parents’ oak, a wish to look like the city even if the city was a forty-minute drive — those are ordinary wishes. Lane and Henredon were not swindles. They were factories answering a mood. The swindle, when there was one, was the photograph of lacquer on a board that could not take a second life. Gloss on paper is a year. Gloss on a chest you can refinish is a finish.

Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, does not do Memphis and should not be asked to. The company’s own copy still says hardwood, no particleboard, and dates Bradley Lumber Co. to 1902; that date is company copy until a primary record sits beside it [CITE NEEDED]. The useful contrast, in a 1980s essay, is not a moral about color. It is a mechanical one. A lacquered hardwood case can be ugly for a decade and handsome when black comes back, because the case is still a case. A brass-colored tube around a void cannot come back as anything but scrap. The shop that refuses the void is not above fashion. It is beside it, staining oak darker when the floor wants dark, and leaving you a board when the floor wants something else.

Memphis ended. The mall table did not get a dissolution date. It got a basement. If you are keeping one object from the glossy binge, keep the chest that can take a new polish, or the brass that is brass on a wood that is wood. Let the cocktail table go to the person who wants a prop. Props are allowed. They are not furniture. Furniture is what is left when the downlight is off and the plant ring is still there, and you can still set a drink on something that does not wobble.

item.title: Chippy Paint, Washable White, and the Factory Vintage
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The sofa is white and it has been washed, which is the only reason it is still in the room. The slipcover comes off in pieces you learn by doing, not by a diagram. Under it: a body that has taken children and a dog and a decade of Sunday papers. Beside it, a side table with paint so thin the wood shows through in a pattern that is not a pattern — real wear, from real years, before anyone called it a look. A chandelier with missing crystals hangs a little crooked. Roses on a pillow that has faded to the color of a receipt. This is the room Rachel Ashwell was aiming at, or close to it: English flea-market childhood, California light, a house that looked as if it had always been slightly undone on purpose.

Photo cue: FFF-05a — White slipcovered sofa, slightly crumpled, a genuinely worn painted table, a modest chandelier; daylight, no florist’s rose dump. Rights: original interior or a documented 1990s Shabby Chic shop photograph, licensed.

Rachel Ashwell opened a Shabby Chic store in Santa Monica in 1989. That is the company’s date. The Los Angeles Times, on October 19, 1996, said she rented in Malibu in 1988 and opened a shop within a year. Both can be true in the way retail lives are true: a rental, then a sign. The book Shabby Chic came from Harper in 1996 and taught a country that had not been to the shop how to talk: slipcovers, chippy paint, roses, washable white sofas, chandeliers that had already lived. Ashwell’s childhood, as she has told it, was English flea markets — objects with a prior, bought cheap, used hard. The store sold that prior as a present tense.

The look was not “distressed” as a verb the factory did to a new suite. It was a pile of things that had already been used, then covered in a cloth you could clean. That distinction is the whole essay. A washed white sofa is a practical luxury. A new dresser beaten with chains in a plant to impersonate a washed life is a SKU. Both got called shabby chic after a while. Only one of them had been a shopkeeper’s habit.

The book made the habit portable. Harper’s 1996 volume is a how-to that does not apologize for chipped paint or a sofa that looks slept on. It also, by existing, gave factories a mood board. Once a look has page numbers, a plant can hit those page numbers. Slipcovers went from a California shop practice to a department-store SKU: white, cream, a faded rose, a denim that was trying to be English without the rain. Chandeliers followed, many of them new, already missing nothing, the “rescue” applied as a dark wax. The shop had sold objects with a prior. The floor sold the prior as a finish.

Status, in the Santa Monica years and then in the catalog years, was inherited ease you had in fact purchased. You were not the black-lacquer person. You were not the Mediterranean-oak person. You had taste that looked accidental, which is the hardest taste to fake and therefore the one retail most wanted to productize. White said money that did not need to show dirt because someone would wash the cover. Chippy paint said the family had been in the house long enough to neglect a table. Roses said England without a ticket. A chandelier in a bungalow said you had rescued something from a bigger life. The claim was softness and time. Time, again, is the finish a store cannot quite stock.

Photo cue: FFF-05b — 1996 Harper *Shabby Chic* cover or a period shop interior, Santa Monica; fair-use thumbnail in the editor’s file, rights before a public page.

Retail took the habit and made a department. Department stores hung slipcovers. Catalogs sold “vintage white” bedroom groups that had never been vintage. Restoration Hardware, founded in Eureka, California, in 1979 by Stephen Gordon — later RH, later Gary Friedman’s catalog theater — ran its own early distress: hardware-store romance, weathered wood, a past you could order. That is a cousin of Ashwell, not a twin. Magnolia farmhouse, after Chip and Joanna Gaines’s Fixer Upper (HGTV, 2013–2018), is another cousin: white paint, old wood, a Waco light, shiplap. Cousins share a pale wall and a wish for the prior. They do not share a slipcover philosophy, and they do not share an English flea market. Flattening them into one “farmhouse white” is how the 2010s thought. It is not how the objects were born.

The hangover is already in the warehouses and on the curb. Factory-distressed “vintage” bedroom suites in gray-white: a new case, a gray wash, edges sanded to a uniform honesty, hardware darkened as if a hand had been there. The chippy look as a SKU. You can date these suites to a band of years after the book, after the shop, after the word had left Santa Monica and gone to a plant that could distress on a schedule. The gray-white is not Ashwell’s washed rose-and-cream. It is a later correction — greige thinking applied to a romantic idea — and it dates faster because it was never trying to be a particular room. It was trying to be a thumbnail.

I have sat on slipcovered sofas that were a kindness. White, in a house with kids, is not a dare if the cover comes off. That is the part of the fad that was furniture. Washable is a virtue magazines under-rank because it does not photograph as an heirloom. Ashwell ranked it. The part that was a year is the matching painted suite, the rose stencil, the chandelier bought new to look rescued, the word “shabby” printed on a hangtag attached to a box that smelled of the finishing room. People bought those suites because they wanted the ease and the store only sold the picture of ease. That is ordinary. It does not require a sneer. It requires a sorting: which object can take another twenty years of actual neglect, and which object was neglected in a factory at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday.

What ages is a real old painted piece with real wear. The wear is uneven. It is on the corners a hand uses, not on every edge the designer circled. The paint is a history of paints, not one wash. The wood, if you get through, is a wood. You can keep painting it. You can stop. You can strip it and be surprised by pine or by something better. A slipcover that is a slipcover — not upholstery pretending to have a zipper — ages because it can leave. The sofa frame, if it is a frame, can take a second cloth. Most will not be worth that bill. Some will. The ones that will were not the ones sold as a color.

What dates is new furniture beaten in the factory. The uniform chip. The gray-white that matches the wall that matches the Instagram tile. The “antique white” bedroom group still in the carton, the distressing already finished, the story already told. Restoration Hardware’s early weathered look, when it was a look applied to new goods, dates as a catalog year the same way. Magnolia’s later white-and-wood, when it arrived as a kit in a subdivision, dates as a television year. Cousins, again. Each cousin has a hangover. The hangover of shabby chic is the suite that cannot get older because it was born old.

Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, is not a slipcover shop. The company’s own copy still says hardwood, no particleboard, and dates Bradley Lumber Co. to 1902; treat that date as company copy until a primary record sits beside it [CITE NEEDED]. The useful contrast is a case that does not need a beating to have a life. You can paint a hardwood dresser. People will. You can leave it a wood. What you cannot honestly do is sell a new box as a prior. A hardwood shop that refuses to fake the prior is not refusing white sofas. It is refusing the lie about time. Ashwell’s better rooms were not a lie. They were a pile of used things and a washable cover. The factory vintage is the lie that came after, when the pile would not scale.

If you are keeping one object from this binge, keep the table that was already tired before the book, or the sofa whose cover you have actually put in a machine. Let the gray-white suite go to the person who wants a guest room to look decided by Friday. Decided-by-Friday is allowed. It is also a year. The chandelier can stay if the crystals are glass and the crooked is yours. Bought crooked is a different object. One of them is a house. The other is a shipment.

item.title: Shiplap, Barn Doors, and the Subdivision Farm
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The sliding door is off the track. It is pine, or a pine veneer, black strap hardware, a handle that is a handle the way jewelry is a handle — meant to be seen, not particularly meant to be used twice a day by a person in a hurry. Behind it: a water heater, or a pantry, or a pair of coats. The house is a 2016 spec build in a county that grows more garages than hay. The walls in the living room are shiplap, painted white, running past a television the size of a small door. A Mason jar holds spoons. Another holds flowers that came from the supermarket in a rubber band. This is modern farmhouse as it arrived in the rooms that had never had a farm: a hardware store of signs, a softness of white, a black line of iron to keep the white from floating away.

Photo cue: FFF-06a — Interior barn door off its track, black strap hardware, white shiplap; spec-house daylight, water heater or pantry visible. Rights: original documentary interior, faces optional and unposed.

Fixer Upper went out as a pilot on HGTV on May 23, 2013, and ran through April 3, 2018. Chip and Joanna Gaines, Waco, Texas. The show did not invent white paint or old wood. It gave a lot of people permission to put those two facts in the same sentence and call the sentence a house. Shiplap — boards with a rabbet, historically a way to weatherproof a wall or a hull — became a living-room skin. Sliding barn doors became interior architecture. Mason jars became lighting and storage and a kind of sincerity you could buy by the case. Black iron. White paint on old wood. Magnolia Market, in Waco, sold the objects that photographed like the show. The show sold the town. The town sold a weekend.

Restoration Hardware had been working a parallel industrial for a longer time. Stephen Gordon founded the company in Eureka, California, in 1979; later it became RH under Gary Friedman and a catalog that treated warehouse salvage as a luxury vocabulary: reclaimed wood tables, zinc, iron beds, a scale that implied you had a loft even if you had a great room. Those catalogs were heavier than the show. They sold a factory floor as a living room and charged for the square footage of the photograph. Pottery Barn and West Elm — Williams-Sonoma’s other rooms — sold a lighter industrial: metal bases, Edison bulbs, a “workshop” stool, tables that read as factory without requiring a factory. The 2010s put these cousins in the same house. Farmhouse was the walls and the jars. Industrial was the table and the lamp. Together they were a subdivision style with a name: modern farmhouse, which is to a farm what a food court is to a kitchen.

The style left the living room and went onto the elevation. Board-and-batten, black window frames, a porch that had never held a tractor, a metal roof on a house that was otherwise vinyl. Builders learned the word because buyers pointed at the show. A plan that had been “Craftsman” in 2006 became “farmhouse” in 2015 with a paint deck and a different door. That is not a crime against architecture. It is how production housing wears a year. The furniture had to keep up with the siding. Black iron inside, white oak or white paint, a table that looked as if it had been dragged from a barn that the lot had never included.

Status was authenticity you could schedule. You were not the Tuscan-granite person of 2004. You were not the black-lacquer person of 1987. You had discovered honesty: wood that looked used, metal that looked like work, a door that looked like it had closed on animals. The animals were metaphorical. The door was on a closet. That does not make the buyer a fool. Television is a more efficient catalog than a catalog, and Fixer Upper was a good catalog. People wanted a house that felt kinder than the granite blob and less temporary than a beige rental. White paint is a kindness. A heavy table is a kindness. The fashion was in the jewelry and in the claim that a ranch in a cul-de-sac had always been this rural.

Photo cue: FFF-06b — Magnolia Market or a period *Fixer Upper* interior still (licensed), or an RH catalog spread of a reclaimed table and zinc; caption must name the source, not “a farmhouse.”

Retail had layers. At the top: actual old wood with a job — a factory cart that had been a cart, a table whose top had been a floor, a zinc that had been a counter. RH, at its better moments, sold some of that, and sold a lot of new goods that impersonated it at a price that felt like salvage even when it was production. In the middle: Pottery Barn’s industrial dining, West Elm’s metal-and-wood, the Magnolia SKUs that a visitor could carry out. At the bottom: the barn-door kit from a big box, the foam “shiplap” or the MDF plank with a painted bevel, the Mason-jar pendant with a reproduction cage, the “reclaimed look” table whose grain was a print. IKEA and Wayfair and Amazon filled the bottom without needing Waco. They needed a filter named rustic.

The hangover is already built into houses that are not ten years old. Barn doors on interior closets in 2019 new-builds — off the track, as this one is, or never quite closing on a bathroom that needed a door that sealed. Shiplap in a ranch that never had a ship, or a barn, or a reason for a horizontal line except that the television show had one. Black interior doors in a house whose exterior is beige vinyl. A sliding door across a pantry that makes a noise at 6 a.m. Hardware as jewelry: straps, arrows, a cast “handmade” that came in a plastic bag. The jewelry dates. The drywall was always drywall.

What ages is actual old wood with a job. A table that was a table, thick enough to plane. A beam that holds something. A board that was outside and is now a mantel and still looks like it has weather in it, because it does. White paint on that board is a decision you can reverse, or live with, or refresh. Black iron that is iron, on a piece that needs iron, ages the way a hinge ages. What dates is the hardware as jewelry — the barn-door strap on a closet, the mason jar that is doing lamp work it was not blown for, the shiplap that is a wallpaper of wood, the word “farmhouse” on a sofa tag in a room that has underfloor heating and an HOA.

I have stood in kitchens where the island was a real hardwood top and the door to the pantry was a barn kit, and the top will outlast the kit by a generation if anyone bothers to oil it. That pairing is the 2010s in one glance. The wish was weight and story. The purchase was often story applied to a house that already had HVAC. Chip and Joanna painted a lot of real rooms in Waco. The copies painted a look onto a floor plan that had been drawn before the show existed. Both acts are allowed. Only one of them is a renovation. The other is a costume on a spec.

Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, does not sell a barn door and does not need a Magnolia adjective. The company’s own copy still says hardwood, no particleboard, and dates Bradley Lumber Co. to 1902; that date is company copy until a primary record sits beside it [CITE NEEDED]. The useful contrast in this decade is a top that can take the white paint off. Farmhouse fashion used wood as a feeling. A hardwood shop uses wood as a thickness. When the feeling moves — and it has already moved, toward quieter oak, toward a beige that is ashamed of the word farmhouse — the thickness is still there. The strap hardware is in a junk drawer with the oil-rubbed bronze grapes from the Tuscan year.

Modern farmhouse as a subdivision style will have a second life in the resale photos, the way Tuscan did: a little apologetic, a little stubborn, a sliding door that the next owner will take down and not know where to put. Take the door down if it does not close. Keep the table if the table is wood through the top. Leave the Mason jars to the pantry, where a jar is a jar. The show ended in 2018. The houses did not. That is the ordinary afterlife of a fashion that got into the walls. Walls are harder to return than a coffee table. That is why this fad will haunt longer than Memphis, and with less color.

Photo cue: FFF-06c — 2010s spec living room: white shiplap, black iron coffee table, Mason-jar cluster; or a curb pile with a barn door and a strap hinge. No sneer in the caption.

item.title: Quiet Oak, Loud Cart
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The table is pale oak and there is nothing on it except a linen runner that looks as if it were ironed once and then allowed to forget. The walls are plaster, or a paint that wants to be plaster. No monogram. No metal word. No clock that says the brand of the clock. A sofa in a cloth that photographs as oatmeal. The listing, if this were a listing, would say quiet luxury and mean 2023. Two miles away, in a walk-up, a different oak table is coming out of a carton: the grain repeats, the edge is paper, the cams are in a plastic bag. Same word, oak, two objects. One of them is a refusal. One of them is a cart.

Photo cue: FFF-07a — Pale oak table, linen, plaster or plaster-like wall, no logos; opposite frame or the far side of the same shot: a flat-pack oak-print table half out of the box, cam locks visible.

Quiet luxury, as a phrase, is a 2022–2023 fashion tag. The Row. Loro Piana. The costumes on Succession, which taught a wide audience that the richest people in a fiction might dress as if they had forgotten to dress. No logo was the logo. The phrase migrated into rooms the way fashion phrases do: linen, oak, plaster, a brown that is ashamed of being a color. Shelter feeds and the better catalogs picked it up because it was a useful correction after a decade of farmhouse jewelry and a shorter binge of blush velvet. The room that refused a claim became a claim. That is not hypocrisy. That is how status works when it gets tired of shouting.

Fast furniture is older than the phrase that scolds it. IKEA arrived in the United States in 1985, Plymouth Meeting, Pennsylvania, and made a philosophy of the flat box: furniture for a life that moves. Wayfair, 2002, made a philosophy of the infinite aisle: every silhouette, every finish, a filter, a truck. Amazon put a dresser in the same cart as the paper towels. Those three are not one speed. IKEA still designs a system and a store you can walk. Wayfair designs a search. Amazon designs a default. The 18-month dresser is not a statistic I can publish with a straight face — I have no panel data in this file — but it is a type. You have seen it. A first apartment, a first kid, a move that requires the piece to come apart, a corner that swells after a spilled bottle, a listing that says “free, you haul, missing a drawer.” The type is real. The market-share number would be a decoration. I will not decorate.

Status now splits. One kind of status is the refusal: no logo, no hardware that reads as a year, a table that looks as if it had always been there and had never needed to announce a shop. That status is expensive when it is real, because real oak and real linen and a plaster wall that is plaster cost what they cost. The other kind of status is the cart full of lookalikes: the quiet-luxury thumbnail at a Thursday price, the oatmeal sofa that is a color, the oak that is a photograph of oak. Both buyers are trying to look decided. One is paying for silence. One is paying for a picture of silence. I will not rank their characters. I will rank the objects when they have to move.

Photo cue: FFF-07b — *Succession* still or The Row / Loro Piana campaign image used as fashion context (licensed), beside a Wayfair or IKEA oak-look dining table in a real small apartment. Caption must not invent a sales figure.

Retail did not wait to be scolded. The same companies that sold barn doors in 2016 sold “organic modern” and “quiet” oak in 2023, sometimes from the same warehouse, a different finish code. RH had already been in the linen-and-scale business. Pottery Barn softened the iron. West Elm put a pale wood on the same tapered leg that had been walnut-print in 2012. IKEA, which had never needed a luxury phrase, already had birch and white and a table you could carry. The phrase did not create a new factory. It created a new caption. Captions are cheap. Oak is not.

The fashion houses that originated the silence were not in the dresser business. The Row and Loro Piana sell cloth and a refusal. Rooms borrowed the refusal because rooms were tired of hardware that shouted 2016. A plaster wall and a linen sofa are a pleasant correction. They become a fad when the correction is sold as a personality. A person who wants less metal on the cabinets is not performing quiet luxury. A person who buys a logo-less look as a kit, down to the book on the table that is not being read, is performing it. Both rooms can be comfortable. Only one of them needs the phrase to stay standing.

A quiet oak table that is actually oak can be pale this year and darker later. You can oil it. You can scratch it and call the scratch a year of dinners. You can hate the present fashion for raw wood and still have a table. A quiet oak table that is a photograph of oak cannot change its mind. The paper is the design. When the pale wash dates — and pale washes date, they just date softly — there is nothing to sand toward. Paint is an option. Paint on paper is a painted photograph. The cart will take it to the curb with less guilt than it took the Mediterranean hutch, because nobody ever believed the paper was a grandmother.

What ages, in this argument, is almost rude in its simplicity. Solid hardwood, or a thick honest veneer over a stable core, named as such. A finish you can name. Joinery you can get back into. Linen that is linen and can be cleaned or replaced. Plaster that is plaster, which is a wall, not a furniture essay, except that the wall is how the furniture is being sold. What dates is the phrase used as a product: “quiet luxury” on a tag, a logo-less look that is a SKU, a beige that exists to photograph as restraint. Fast furniture dates on a shorter clock because it was built for the clock — the lease, the move, the next filter.

The hangover of quiet luxury will be quieter than the hangover of barn doors, which is the danger. A beige room does not look foolish in a photograph even when it looks like every other beige room. Fast furniture’s hangover is louder and more honest: the dresser that cannot be moved twice, the paper edge gone white, the cam lock stripped, the swell at the sink. People will keep buying both, because rooms have to be lived in now. A student needs a table before an heirloom. A person who just got the job that Succession was parodying may want the silence and be able to pay for it. Neither need is a moral test. The test is whether the object can survive the end of the caption.

Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, sells hardwood that does not need the phrase. That is the useful sentence, and it is enough. The company’s own copy still says no particleboard and dates Bradley Lumber Co. to 1902; treat the date as company copy until a primary record sits beside it [CITE NEEDED]. I am not turning a shop in Warren into The Row. I am pointing at a mechanical fact the fashion phrase keeps trying to steal: quiet is easier when the table is oak through the thickness. A photograph of oak has to keep talking. It talks in the repeat of the grain, in the chip at the corner, in the way you cannot refinish a picture.

I have watched people unpack both kinds of table in the same week. The oak one needed two people and a pad. The paper one needed an Allen key and a movie on a phone. Both dinners happened. Both rooms looked finished for a night. In five years the question will not be which owner had better taste. It will be which table is still a table. Fashion will have a new phrase by then. It may be loud again. It may be another silence. The hardwood will not have needed the memo. The carton table will have needed a second carton, or a curb.

If you want the refusal, buy the refusal in material, not in a caption. If you want the cart, buy the cart and admit the year — eighteen months or five, whatever your life actually does. Years are allowed. A house that is only captions is a feed you happen to sleep in. The linen can stay wrinkled. The runner can stay off. The table, if it is a table, does not require a logo to refuse a logo. It requires a board.

item.title: The Board That Was a Photograph
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The dresser lists to the left because the corner has gone soft. You can see the substrate where the paper tore: a pale crumb, not quite wood, not quite anything you would name at a lumberyard. A cam lock spins in its hole and does not catch. The piece has moved house once. The second move is the one it will not survive, and everyone in the room already knows it. On the other wall, an older chest — oak, heavy, a drawer that sticks in August — waits as if it had been waiting since a different administration. Two storage technologies. One of them was designed to be furniture for a while. The other was designed to be furniture.

Photo cue: FFF-08a — Particleboard dresser, paper oak torn at a corner, cam lock in the foreground; opposite or beside it, a solid-oak chest, drawers open enough to show a dovetail or a wood runner. Daylight, no brand on the new piece unless it is already there.

Max Himmelheber, in Germany, developed particleboard in the 1930s and 1940s — a board made of chips and resin, waste wood given a job. The patent is often cited as 1932 or 1933. I do not have the number in this file. [CITE NEEDED] Postwar reconstruction needed houses and the furniture to put in them, and a board that did not require a clean log was a serious answer to a serious shortage. Particleboard is not a moral failure. It is an industrial success. The lie arrived later, when the board put on a photograph of oak and went to a store that sold “wood” to people who wanted wood.

IKEA made the board respectable as a philosophy, not only as a price. Furniture for the many, flat in a carton, cheap enough to leave. The 1985 American opening, Plymouth Meeting, did not invent the substrate. It taught a country that the substrate could be a life: student years, first jobs, rooms that would be abandoned on purpose. That teaching was generous. It still is, for the years it fits. The trouble is the years it does not fit — the dresser asked to be an heirloom, the cabinet asked to live beside a sink, the “oak” asked to take a refinish. Philosophy and joinery are not the same department.

Veneer, laminate, and paper are three different skins, and the trade has spent decades hoping you will not sort them. A real veneer is a thin slice of actual wood, glued to a core. It can be beautiful. It can be repaired by a person who still knows how. It is not solid, and it should not be sold as solid. A laminate is a plastic sheet, often with a photograph or a print of wood, bonded to a board; it laughs at a coffee cup and fails at a chip. Paper, in the cheap case goods, is a printed grain rolled onto particleboard or MDF and edged in a plastic strip the color of the print. You cannot sand a photograph. You can only live with it until the edge lifts.

Photo cue: FFF-08b — Three samples on a bench: true wood veneer, plastic laminate with a repeat grain, paper oak on particleboard with the core showing; include a ruler. Shop light, not a lifestyle pour.

California’s Air Resources Board wrote formaldehyde rules that actually changed what could be sold — a rare furniture fact with a regulator’s name on it. If you name a phase (CARB Phase 2, or the later federal alignment), attach a date from the rule text. [CITE NEEDED] I will not invent the year on this page. What can be said without a press release is that the board in the corner of the room is not only a style problem. It is a chemistry problem the state decided to treat as air. That is a better sentence than any brand claim about “clean.”

The joints are the other honesty test. A screw-cam lock — the little steel barrel, the bolt that draws two boards together — is a brilliant packing idea. It is a poor life idea. Every move loosens it. Every over-tightening strips it. A dresser built on cams is a dresser built for the first assembly, not for the third. Swelling at the sink is the domestic version of the same physics: particleboard drinks, and once it has drunk, it does not return to the dimension the cam was cut for. The corner goes pale, then furry, then soft. People keep using the drawers because the drawers still hold shirts. Holding shirts is not the same as being a case.

Solid hardwood is not a hymn. It is a set of operations you can still do. You can resand a top. You can re-glue a broken rail. You can replace a runner. You can hate the stain and change it. You can inherit the chest and not inherit the year it was stained. None of that makes the owner virtuous. It makes the object available to a second life. A lot of old solid pieces are ugly, under-scaled, or repaired badly. Keep them or don’t. The option is the point. The particleboard dresser in the listing does not offer the option. It offers a first impression and a weight that surprises you when you try to be careful with it. The weight is glue and crumb. It is not a promise.

Status has attached itself to both materials, in different decades, which is worth saying without a sneer. In 1974 a carved oak suite was status. Some of those suites were oak. Some were oak-colored board. In 2004 a granite kitchen with “cherry” cabinets was status, and a lot of the cherry was a print. In 2023 a quiet oak table is status, and the table may be oak or a photograph of oak. Buyers are not the villains of this essay. Buyers are busy. The villain, when there is one, is a caption that says wood and means paper. IKEA, at its clearer moments, has been more honest about the board than the mall brands that wrapped the same board in a heritage typeface. Honesty is a catalog choice. It is also a hinge.

The hangover is the trash-day object I keep seeing in the same hour as a 1970s table nobody wants to carry. Paper lifted at the drawer edge, white tooth of the core, a cam on the sidewalk. Next to it, sometimes, the oak table. Carry the table. Leave the tooth. The street is not sentimental. It is sentimental about the possibility of a second use. Particleboard that has swollen has used its life. Solid wood that is ugly has not.

Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, prints “no particleboard” on its own product copy. That is a contrast, not a hymn. The same family of copy dates Bradley Lumber Co. to 1902; treat the date as company copy until a primary record sits beside it [CITE NEEDED]. A shop that refuses the board is refusing a set of operations it cannot reverse later: the cam, the paper, the swell. It is not refusing cheap furniture as a class, and it should not be asked to sneer at the student who needs the carton. The student is right about the carton. The carton is wrong about the word oak.

What ages is the piece you can get back into: a solid top, a joint that is a joint, a skin that is wood if it claims to be wood. What dates is the photograph used as a species. Grain that repeats every eighteen inches. An edge band that peels. A finish that is the print. Fashion will keep needing that photograph, because the photograph is how a new year gets on a truck at a price a new year can stand. A hardwood shop will keep making a top. You can buy from both without lying to yourself if you know which purchase is a while and which is a chest. A while is allowed. A house that is only whiles is a sequence of cartons that you happen to sleep between.

Himmelheber’s board did a job. The job was reconstruction, then plenty, then a philosophy of leaving. Those are real jobs. The job it cannot do is pretend, after the paper tears, that it was a tree you could meet again with sandpaper. The oak chest on the other wall does not need that pretense. It needs wax, or a plane, or to be left alone. Leave it alone if you want. The option is the furniture.

Photo cue: FFF-08c — Curb in one town: swollen particleboard dresser, paper oak, a loose cam; a solid table or chest nearby if the street offers it. Caption names the materials, not the owners.

item.title: Color Cycles — Avocado to Greige
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The refrigerator is avocado and the range is harvest gold, and they were sold as a pair. The laminate on the counters tries to split the difference and fails. Someone has left a teak cutting board on that laminate, and the teak is the only object in the room that does not look like a year. You can date the kitchen to a band of years in the 1970s without opening a cabinet. The wood does not help you. The appliances do.

Photo cue: FFF-09a — 1970s American kitchen, harvest-gold range and avocado refrigerator in the same frame; period manufacturer brochure or Library of Congress interior if rights clear.

Paint is the cheapest way a house changes its mind. A gallon of alkyd in 1973 cost less than a dinette and covered more surface. That is why color cycles run through kitchens first and furniture second. The wall can be wrong for a weekend. A sofa dyed to match the wall is wrong for the life of the fabric. The hangover is always the same: the paint gets rolled over, and the matching furniture sits in the garage because it still works and no longer belongs.

Harvest gold and avocado were not accidents of taste. They were appliance colors with names on chips, pushed through General Electric, Frigidaire, and Sears into rooms that had just finished with turquoise and pink. Gold read as sun and wheat; avocado read as the outdoors brought inside after a decade of white-and-chrome kitchens. Both colors photographed as warmth in the catalogs. In person, under a fluorescent shop light, they went muddy. That muddiness is what people remember now, and it is unfair to the better rooms — a walnut table under a gold range still looks like a table. The gold range looks like 1974.

By the early 1980s the gold had to go. Dusty rose and mauve arrived as a correction that was also a fashion. They sat on brass, on pickled oak, on the gray-mauve carpet that department stores rolled out by the acre. A mauve sofa in a 1986 Ethan Allen gallery was not a joke. It was a finished thought: softness after harvest, femininity after earth-tone masculinity, a room that wanted to look expensive without looking brown. The same sofa in 1994 looked like a bridesmaid. Color does that. It does not wait for the springs to fail.

Photo cue: FFF-09b — mid-1980s dusty-rose living room, brass lamp, pickled-oak wall unit; department-store or shelter-magazine spread.

Hunter green and burgundy took the 1990s by the collar. Ralph Lauren Home had already taught a generation that a room could dress like a study. Pottery Barn and the mall versions followed with forest green slipcovers, oxblood leather club chairs, and gold-on-green wallpaper borders that no one has forgiven. The signal was club, lodge, money that had read a book. A cherry entertainment center stained almost black sat under a hunter-green wall and called the whole thing traditional. Traditional, in that decade, meant a color story you could buy in one Saturday. The wood, if it was actually cherry, still had a chance. The painted pine “country” suite in the same green did not.

Then the 2000s wanted Tuscany. Not Tuscany the place — Tuscany the paint aisle. Faux-finished gold plaster, grape-and-vine iron, a dining set with a distressed ochre base and a faux-travertine top. Home Depot and Lowe’s sold the glaze kits; furniture floors sold the matching chairs. The status claim was travel and appetite. You had been somewhere warm, or you wished to look as if you had. A solid oak table with a clear finish could live through that wish. A dining set whose entire identity was the ochre glaze could not. When the glaze dated, the set dated. There was nothing underneath the costume except MDF and a hope.

Millennial pink is the first color in this list that arrived as a joke people meant. Around 2016 the phrase stuck to a dusty, slightly dirty rose that was not quite 1980s mauve and not quite ballet. Pantone’s Rose Quartz, paired with Serenity for 2016, gave the trade a chip to point at [CITE NEEDED for the exact pairing language on the Pantone release]. Instagram did the rest. Blush velvet chairs, rose-gold hardware, a sofa in a pink that photographers liked at 10 a.m. The furniture that took the year hardest was the cheap upholstery: a blush modular that existed to be photographed next to a monstera. Two lease cycles later it reads as a filter. A walnut credenza photographed in the same apartment does not.

Greige is the apology. Agreeable Gray, Sherwin-Williams SW 7029, became a default in the 2010s the way builder-beige had been a default in the 1990s. I will not rank it. Paint companies publish “most popular” lists that are marketing documents as much as sales ledgers, and a rank without the method is a story [CITE NEEDED before any claim that Agreeable Gray was the bestselling interior color in any year]. What can be said without a press release is that greige walls — gray with enough yellow or brown to keep a room from going cold — showed up in staging, in open houses, in the rental units that turned over every twelve months. The point of greige is that it refuses to be a year. That is also how it becomes one. A whole street of Agreeable Gray interiors is as dated as a street of hunter green, only quieter about it.

Photo cue: FFF-09c — 2010s staged living room, greige walls, white trim, gray-taupe sectional; real-estate listing photograph with rights, or a paint-chip card of SW 7029 beside a sofa arm.

The 2020s reached for terracotta and sage the way the 1970s reached for gold and avocado: earth again, after a decade of gray. Sage cabinets, terracotta planters, a rust velvet chair that wants to be a desert. Sherwin-Williams, Benjamin Moore, and every private-label big-box chip rack offered a version. Furniture followed in bouclé the color of oatmeal and in “organic modern” oak that had been brushed and then stained just enough to look like a mood board. Some of that oak is oak. Some of it is a printed grain on a substrate that will not take a second finish. The color cycle does not care which. It will move on either way.

Here is the mechanic, and it is not mysterious. Paint is fashion you can reverse with a weekend and a drop cloth. Upholstery is fashion you reverse with a check. Case goods finished in the color of the year are fashion you reverse only if the substrate will accept a new coat — solid wood will; a vinyl wrap will not, not honestly. The objects that date fastest are the ones whose whole argument was the chip. A harvest-gold dinette whose plastic seats were molded in that gold has no second life except irony. A maple table that sat under harvest-gold walls can be wiped, oiled, and left alone.

Status works the same way as the chip, only slower to admit it. The 1970s gold kitchen said modern plenty: new appliances, a house that had been updated since the wedding. Mauve said softness and a kind of mall prosperity. Hunter green said you had taste that came from a catalog with a crest. Tuscan gold said you cooked. Millennial pink said you were online in the right year. Greige said you were not trying, which is the most expensive thing to try. Terracotta and sage say you have recovered from gray and would like to be well. None of these claims is wicked. They are just claims, and they expire.

The hangover is visible in any Midwestern basement and any Facebook Marketplace radius around a college town. Avocado refrigerators that still run. A mauve sleeper sofa with a broken pull-bar. A hunter-green wing chair whose velvet has polished to a slick at the headrest. A faux-finished Tuscan buffet that will not die because the particleboard is still structurally polite. A blush velvet chair listed as “mid-century” by a seller who means “I bought it in 2017.” Greige sectionals the size of a carport, too heavy to move, too recent to throw away, already the color of last decade’s open house.

What ages is not “neutral,” which is just a cycle that pretends to sit out the dance. What ages is a finish that belongs to the wood and a color that belongs to pigment, not to a campaign. An oil-rubbed walnut table from the 1960s still looks like walnut. A painted pine armoire in 1998 hunter green looks like 1998 unless you strip it, and stripping painted pine is a penance, not a project. A leather club chair in an actual brown — not oxblood, not cognac-as-a-hashtag — will scuff and then look used, which is different from looking finished.

Photo cue: FFF-09d — oil-rubbed walnut dining table, no matching wall color, daylight; object-only, no lifestyle staging.

A hardwood shop in a small town does not issue a color of the year. Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, sells solid hardwood and says so; the company’s own copy also places Bradley Lumber Co. at 1902, which should be treated as company copy until a primary record sits next to it [CITE NEEDED]. The useful contrast is not moral. It is mechanical. A table that is maple or oak through the top can be refinished when the walls change. A table whose top is a photograph of oak cannot. Paint will keep cycling. That is what paint is for. The mistake is asking the sofa to cycle with it, then being surprised when the sofa becomes the thing you cannot afford to be wrong about.

I have stood in kitchens where the cabinets were still the 1970s oak and the walls had been three colors since. The cabinets were fine. They had been fine under gold, under white, under greige. Someone had wanted to replace them because a television show had replaced cabinets. The oak did not care. The show will have a new color next season. The cabinets will still be oak.

If you are keeping a piece, keep the piece whose color is in the material. If you are indulging a year, indulge it in a gallon, a pillow, a lamp whose shade you can throw away. The harvest-gold range was honest about what it was: an appliance with a fashion skin, meant to be replaced when the compressor died. The harvest-gold sofa pretended to be furniture. That pretense is the whole cycle. It will run again in terracotta, and then in whatever name they give the next gray.
