item.title: The Sectional as Fad Architecture
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The floor drops. Not a step you notice from the hallway — a square cut out of the living room, maybe fifteen feet on a side, lined in fabric, with a table in the middle that has nowhere to go except down. You sit, and the rest of the house rises around your shoulders. Conversation happens at the level of knees if someone remains standing. That is the Miller House pit in Columbus, Indiana, finished in 1957: Eero Saarinen on the house, Alexander Girard on the interiors, Dan Kiley on the grounds. The pit is Girard’s. The house now belongs to Newfields, the Indianapolis Museum of Art, and you tour it on their terms.

Photo cue: FFF-10a — Miller House conversation pit, Columbus, Indiana; Newfields / IMA photograph, Girard textiles visible, pit roughly square.

A conversation pit is architecture that decided to be furniture, or furniture that decided to be a room. Either way, it is a sectional that cannot be rearranged without a contractor. The Miller version is the one the histories keep because the clients, J. Irwin and Xenia Miller, could afford Saarinen and Girard and a town that already understood modern as a civic project. The pit is specific: built-in, upholstered, scaled to a house that was never going to be flipped. It is also the ancestor of every sunken living room in a 1970s subdivision, and of every modular cloud that now occupies the square footage a dining table used to claim.

Saarinen, later, is said to have worried that the pit had become a cliché [CITE NEEDED — the remark circulates in secondary write-ups; I have not got his sentence in hand]. If he said it, he was watching the copy, not the original. Copies are how a private solution becomes a fad. By the late 1960s and through the 1970s, builders were dropping living rooms a half-flight and ringing the depression with tufted benches, shag, and a fireplace that had to be stepped down to as if it were a shrine. The suburban pit said: we have a great room, we have conversation, we are not our parents’ sofa-and-two-chairs. It also said: we have poured a furniture arrangement into concrete and called it design.

Those pits aged the way built-ins age when the fabric dates. You cannot slide them to the wall. You cannot sell them with the house unless the next buyer wants a conversation. A lot of them were filled in. The fill is a hangover you can still find if you know what a patched floor looks like in a 1974 ranch — a rectangle of newer hardwood or a change in the pad under the carpet, the ghost of a social idea.

The 1980s and 1990s did not abandon the sectional. They stood it back up and sold it as a leather pit that lived at grade. Rooms To Go opened in 1991, Jeffrey Seaman’s Florida chain, and made the leather sectional a package: sofa plus chaise plus ottoman plus a lamp that matched the tag. The signal was plenty and ease. You could seat eight for a game. You could sleep a cousin. The leather was often corrected and sprayed, and it sat on frames that were not trying to be heirlooms. That is not an insult. It is a product. The hangover is the cracked arm and the chaise that no longer latches to the corner, listed locally for a price that assumes someone else still wants that much hide.

Photo cue: FFF-10b — 1990s Rooms To Go–style leather sectional in a tiled great room, oversized ottoman, television as the fourth wall; period catalog or newspaper insert if rights allow.

Restoration Hardware — later RH — launched the Cloud sofa in 2015, a Timothy Oulton design for the company. Deep, slipcovered, modular, the opposite of a tufted club. Architectural Digest and the celebrity-home circuit put Clouds in rooms that already had a publicist [CITE NEEDED for any specific AD celebrity interior you name; the coverage exists as a class]. The Cloud is a pit that forgot to sink. It achieves the same social diagram — many bodies, low, facing inward or facing a screen — by volume instead of excavation. It eats the room the way the 1970s pit ate the floor. The difference is you can, in theory, unclip a module and move it. In practice the Cloud is bought as an expanse of cushions and it stays.

Status moved with the construction type. The Miller pit said: we commissioned this. The 1970s sunken room said: the builder included this, and we are current. The Rooms To Go leather pit said: we can seat the playoffs. The Cloud said: we have the same sofa as the people in the magazine, and we have the square footage to let it sprawl. None of those sentences is about lumbar support. A sectional is almost never about sitting well. It is about occupying. It is architecture you finance.

Modular systems tried, at intervals, to be the intelligent version. Harvey Probber’s mid-century modulars, the Italian systems of the 1970s, the grid sofas that could be a bed or a corner — they assumed a owner who would reconfigure. Most owners do not reconfigure. They buy the floor-plan drawing the salesperson sketched on a tablet, then they live inside that drawing until they move. The fad is not the module. The fad is the belief that the module is a plan for the rest of your life.

Photo cue: FFF-10c — RH Cloud or Cloud-type modular in a pale room, modules filling the floor to the window wall; 2010s–2020s shelter photograph, rights dependent.

What dates is scale married to a year. A 1970s pit with original harvest-gold upholstery is a year. A 1990s leather sectional with oak bun feet and a matching recliner is a year. A 2018 cloud in performance linen the color of unbaked bread is already picking up a year, not because the idea is dead but because every staged house on a certain coast used the same idea at once. What ages is a settee that still has a back you can find, a pair of chairs that can turn, a sofa whose arms do not require a room to justify them. Those pieces lose the argument about how many people can lie down at once. They win the argument about whether the room is still a room.

I am not against lying down. I am against a furniture type that pretends it is the only way a living room can mean hospitality. The Miller pit works because the house was drawn around it, because Girard’s textiles and the court of the house give the depression a job. Drop the same idea into a builder great room with a ninety-inch television and you have a trench for snacks. Raise it up, stuff it, call it a cloud, and you have a mattress with opinions. The social claim is identical: we gather. The architectural cost is the rest of the floor.

Retail learned to sell that cost as a feature. The 1970s furniture stores sold “conversation groups.” The 1990s sold “home theater seating.” The 2010s sold “lounge.” Same footprint, new vocabulary. Wayfair and the warehouse clubs added the oversized sectional as a click, delivered in boxes that filled a driveway, assembled by two people who will not speak for an hour. The hangover from that wave is already in the resale apps: sectionals too big for the next apartment, stains on a chaise that was never meant to be re-covered, frames that are stapled webbing and foam. A pit you can return to the shipper is still a pit if it leaves a hole in the room’s budget.

A craft note, without a close. Upholstery is fashion. Frames can be furniture. A hardwood shop — Bradley Brand Furniture in Warren, Arkansas, is one, selling solid hardwood by its own product copy, and dating Bradley Lumber Co. to 1902 in that same copy until a primary record confirms it [CITE NEEDED] — does not solve a sectional. It does not have to. What it can do is refuse to pretend that a plywood box under six yards of polyester is the same class of object as a table you can plane. The sectional’s job is comfort and capacity. When those are honest, the piece is honest. When the piece also claims to be the architecture of the house, it is doing a second job it will be fired from the next time the plan changes.

Photo cue: FFF-10d — filled-in sunken living room in a 1970s ranch, change in flooring visible; documentary photograph, not a staging.

Stand in the Miller House pit if you get the tour. Notice that you are in a designed hole, and that the hole has edges Girard chose. Then go home and look at whatever is eating your rug. If it is a cloud, it is a 2015 idea with a long retail tail. If it is a leather pit from a 1994 Sunday insert, it is a Rooms To Go idea that outlived the insert. If you are lucky enough to have a built-in from a real architect, you have a maintenance problem and a document. The fad is not sitting together. The fad is believing the sofa should be the floor plan. Saarinen’s house still has a pit because the house was the pit’s reason. Most living rooms are not a reason. They are a rectangle, and a rectangle can hold chairs.

item.title: Outdoor Living Spikes
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The chair is iron painted white, the back a morning-glory scroll, and it is sitting on a department-store floor in Los Angeles in 1945 as if the war had not just ended. Brown Jordan — Robert Brown and Hubert Jordan, Pasadena — showed the Morning Glory collection at Bullock’s Wilshire that year. Iron, romantic, a little movie-set. Three years later the same company put Leisure on the floor: aluminum frames, vinyl lace, a lighter idea of sitting outside. The company would keep doing this, collection after collection. Tamiami, by Hall Bradley, came in fashion colors, as if a patio chair were a dress. Outdoor furniture is always a dress. That is why it spikes.

Photo cue: FFF-11a — Brown Jordan Morning Glory iron, 1945, or a documented period installation; Bullock’s Wilshire context if a photograph exists and clears.

Indoor furniture can pretend it is permanent. Outdoor furniture has to admit weather. The admission is what makes it fashionable. A new finish, a new weave, a new claim that this time the stuff will winter over, and the patio is a room again. Then the weave chalks, the sling tears, the fire pit rusts at the seam, and the spike is over. What remains is a stack.

Telescope Casual, upstate New York, folding chairs and tables that knew how to go back in a shed. Lloyd Flanders, Menominee, Michigan, woven furniture that treated wicker as a year-round argument. Redwood decks in the 1970s, the lumber still cheap enough that a suburban lot could grow a platform and call it living. Teak from the contract world and the catalog world, oil-dark, heavy, the status wood of the boat and the club. All-weather wicker later, a resin weave over aluminum, sold as the end of rotting rattan. Each of these is a real product with a real shop behind it. Each of them also rode a spike when the culture decided the yard was a room.

The 1950s and 1960s sold the patio as a California export. Aluminum and vinyl lace photographed well. The drink cart came outside. Status was a pool and the chairs that proved you used it. The 1970s added the redwood deck and the hot-tub surround, cedar and redwood going silver, a wet bar with a pass-through. The 1990s and 2000s added the all-weather package from the warehouse club: a table, six chairs, a market umbrella, a cover that lasted one season. Frontgate, Restoration Hardware, and the big catalogs sold a more expensive version of the same diagram — chaise, fire table, teak that had never seen a shipyard.

Then 2020. People were home. The yard was the only restaurant. CNBC, 17 May 2020, reported the spike with names attached. Overstock’s Ron Hilton said outdoor demand “exploded.” Frontgate’s Lindsay Foster talked chaises and fire pits. Bed Bath & Beyond reported boosts in the same direction. Frontgate’s pool floats were “up over 100 percent,” which is a company figure given to a reporter, not a census, and should be read as such (CNBC, 17 May 2020). I will not invent the rest of the percentages. The qualitative fact is enough: the patio became the spare room, and the spare room got furnished in a hurry.

Photo cue: FFF-11b — spring 2020 patio, new fire pit still in the box or just assembled, delivery carton visible; documentary, not an ad.

A spike has a hangover the way a wedding has a garage. The 2021 and 2022 patios of a certain kind of suburb still hold the evidence: a resin wicker set whose left-arm chair has a broken weave, a propane fire table that is now a table because the burner fouled, an umbrella base the size of a tire and twice as ugly, a stack of folding chairs no one folded. Cheap resin remembers every winter. It chalks. It goes chalk-white and then dirty-white. It is not the vinyl lace of 1948, which at least knew it was festive. It is furniture that was a click, delivered, assembled with a hex key, and then asked to be a room for two summers of a pandemic.

Teak is the counter-example people reach for, and teak can take it, if it is teak. Plantation teak, properly dried, oil or no oil, goes silver and stays structurally itself. A lot of what was sold as teak in the spike years was a thinner story: mixed hardwoods, a teak-colored stain, a tabletop that will cup. All-weather wicker is honest when the aluminum frame is decent and the weave is a replaceable sling idea. It is a costume when the weave is the entire identity and the frame is a tube that kinks. Brown Jordan’s better iron and aluminum, Telescope’s better folding stock, Lloyd Flanders when the weave is still tight — these are outdoor furniture that expected to be refinished or re-strapped. The warehouse set expected to be replaced.

Status outdoors is louder than status in the dining room because the neighbors can see it. A 1970s redwood deck said we built. A 1990s hunter-green resin set said we shopped the club. A 2000s teak-and-stainless package from a catalog said we winter in a place that needs a cover. A 2020 fire pit and a sectional that could have been indoors said we are not going inside, and we have the delivery slot to prove it. The signal is hospitality that faces the street or the fence. When the spike ends, the signal stays out there in the rain, which is why outdoor fashion is crueler than indoor fashion. You cannot hide a dead chaise behind a door.

Photo cue: FFF-11c — 1970s redwood deck, silvered boards, low bench rail; period snapshot or trade photograph.

Retailers love the outdoor spike because it is seasonal and therefore forgivable. Miss this spring and there is next spring. High Point and the casual-furniture shows in Chicago and the Carolinas have long treated outdoor as a line you refresh like ready-to-wear. Hall Bradley’s Tamiami colors were fashion colors. That was the point. You were not supposed to keep the same strap color for twenty years, though the frame might last if you let it. The contemporary equivalent is the powder-coat of the year — sage, terracotta, a black so matte it photographs as a hole — sold on aluminum that is the same extrusion as last year. Paint, again. Fashion, again.

What ages outdoors is mass, joinery, and a finish you can cut back. Wrought iron that can be ground and recoated. Teak that can be sanded. A sling chair whose cloth is a part number. What dates is the novelty of the season: the egg chair in the wrong resin, the faux-wood plastic Adirondack that fades to a bone color no tree ever was, the solar-lantern chandelier over a table that cannot take a real one. The 2020s also produced outdoor rugs in patterns that belong on a phone, and outdoor “sectionals” that brought the cloud problem into the damp. Foam that sits in weather is a faith-based material.

A hardwood shop is not, mostly, in this business. Bradley Brand Furniture in Warren, Arkansas, talks solid hardwood and no particleboard or MDF in its product copy; it also claims the Bradley Lumber line back to 1902, which remains company copy until a primary record is attached [CITE NEEDED]. The quiet contrast is still useful. A maple island in a kitchen will outlast three generations of patio sets bought for the same house. That is not because indoor wood is virtuous. It is because the patio set was never asked to last. It was asked to arrive in time for the first warm Saturday.

Behind a row of college-town rentals the remainder is already out by the bins: four identical resin tables, one missing a leg, two umbrellas with torn vents, a fire bowl filled with rainwater and a single sandal. That is the 2020 spike’s leftover, not the Frontgate chaise in a magazine. Hilton was not wrong that demand exploded. Foster was not wrong that chaises and fire pits moved. The hangover is not their problem. It is the alley’s.

If you are buying outdoor furniture as furniture, buy the frame you can repair and the surface you can refinish. If you are buying a summer, buy a summer and do not call it an investment. Morning Glory iron from 1945, kept painted, is still a chair. A resin stack from 2020 is already a disposal question. The patio will be fashionable again. It always is, the first week the heat breaks. The question is whether you want a dress or a bench. Brown and Jordan, in 1945, were willing to sell you either, and they were clear about the iron. Clarity is the rare outdoor finish.

item.title: Biophilic Wellness Marketing
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The cane is real on the cabinet door and fake on the side panel, and both are being sold as the same idea: you will feel better because a plant once grew. The showroom card says biophilic. The photograph behind the cabinet is a living wall of pothos, lit as if it were a spa. You are looking at a sideboard. The sideboard cannot love you back.

Photo cue: FFF-12a — 2020s furniture-floor display, cane or rattan case piece in front of a living-wall graphic; trade-show or mall gallery, signage visible if it uses the word biophilic.

E.O. Wilson published Biophilia with Harvard University Press in 1984. The word is older. Erich Fromm used it for a love of life as against a love of death, a psychological claim, not a furniture claim. Wilson’s version — an innate orientation toward living systems — gave architects and, later, marketers a scientific-sounding noun. The WELL Building Standard, from the International WELL Building Institute, put biophilia into its Mind concept as qualitative and quantitative features: views, plants, natural materials, patterns. Those are building criteria. They are not a finish schedule for a nightstand.

Furniture retail borrowed the noun the way it borrows every noun that sounds like a benefit. Cane came back. Rattan came back. Bouclé came back, which is wool or a wool-like yarn and has no more to do with a forest than a sweater does. Living-wall photographs appeared behind sofas that had never been near a window that worked. A Furniture Today piece on biophilic merchandising collected the usual executive optimism — plants sell, nature sells, the floor should feel like a refuge [CITE NEEDED for the specific article date and any named CEO; treat those quotes as claims, not as proof that anyone slept better]. A claim in a trade paper is a claim. It is not a trial.

The 1970s had already run a version of this without the word. Avocado and harvest gold were “earth.” Macramé and a spider plant were “bringing the outside in.” The difference now is the certificate language. Wellness is a product category. Biophilic is a SKU adjective. You can buy a “wellness chair” whose only medical property is that it reclines. You can buy a “biophilic” bed whose headboard is a printed grain. The print is often quite good. The word is doing work the print cannot.

Photo cue: FFF-12b — close-up of printed “oak” on particleboard or MDF edge, paper layer visible at the cut; object photography, no lifestyle.

Here is a mechanical fact that does not require Wilson. A solid oak or maple panel is a piece of a tree. It moves with humidity. It can be sanded. It has a smell when you cut it. A laminate with a photograph of oak is a photograph. It does not move the same way. It does not sand. It can look, at ten feet, like the first thing. Wellness marketing prefers the photograph when the photograph is cheaper and the word is the same. That is not a conspiracy. It is a margin.

Cane and rattan are more honest than the print, and they still get dressed up. Real cane, woven into a door or a chair back, is a material with a history in Thonet, in the old porch, in the 1970s import boom, in the 2020s revival. It dries out. It breaks at the edge. It can be re-caned if the frame was built for that. Fashion cane — a plastic weave, or a thin sheet glued to a panel — photographs as the same breeze and then splits. Rattan has the same fork in the road. The 2020s liked both because they photographed as “natural texture” next to a monstera. The monstera is a plant. The chair is a chair. Putting them in one frame does not make the chair a therapy.

Bouclé is a curiosity in this pile. It is a looped yarn. Jean Royère’s mid-century pieces and a long upholstery tradition used it because it takes a curve and hides a seam. The 2010s and 2020s made it a wellness cousin because it looks soft and because a cream bouclé cloud sofa looks like a sheep if you squint. Soft is not biophilia. Soft is upholstery. I like bouclé. I do not like being told it is a forest.

West Elm and CB2 sold the cane and the bouclé as a kit in the late 2010s and early 2020s: a media console with caned doors, a cream chair, a fake olive in a woven basket. Article and the other direct-to-consumer twins ran the same diagram at a slightly different price. The floor card said “natural materials.” The carton, if you read it, sometimes said engineered wood. Both sentences could be true. The customer was buying a feeling that had a SKU. Design Within Reach, after Herman Miller bought it in 2015, could at least point at a cane chair with a designer’s name attached. The mall versions pointed at a photograph of a plant.

Status, in the wellness years, is the appearance of regulation. A WELL feature list on a commercial project is a real checklist with an auditor. A hang-tag on a dresser that says “inspired by biophilic design principles” is a sentence a copywriter can file. The buyer who wants the first thing and gets the second has bought a mood. Moods date. The 2000s Tuscan kitchen was a mood. The 2010s greige open house was a mood. The 2020s sage-and-cane refuge is a mood. You can enjoy a mood. You should know you are in one.

Photo cue: FFF-12c — WELL or similar building-standard diagram versus a furniture hang-tag using “biophilic”; pair the two, rights permitting.

The hangover is already on the resale sites. Cane-panel media consoles with a corner punched in. Rattan peacock chairs that were never as strong as the photograph. Bouclé sofas that have matted on the seat and will not clean because the fiber was a blend meant for a shoot. Living-wall kits behind a sofa, half the pockets empty, the irrigation tray stained. None of this disproves Wilson. Wilson was not selling a console. It disproves the idea that a noun from a Harvard press book can be laminated onto a substrate and still mean what it meant in 1984.

What ages is material that remains itself when the label falls off. A walnut table does not become less like a tree if you stop calling it biophilic. A linen curtain still filters light if you stop calling it a wellness layer. A house with a window that opens still has a window. What dates is the costume of nature: the leaf-print wallpaper that was last year’s botanical, the faux-moss art in a shadow box, the “organic modern” oak that is a brush-and-stain effect on a veneer too thin to sand twice. Organic modern is a catalog heading. It is not a species.

A hardwood shop does not need the heading. Bradley Brand Furniture, Warren, Arkansas, sells solid hardwood and says it does not use particleboard or MDF; that is product copy, and the company’s own materials also place Bradley Lumber Co. at 1902, which should stay labeled as copy until a primary record is on the table [CITE NEEDED]. The contrast is quiet on purpose. An island that is maple through the top does not require a Mind feature to be maple. You can oil it. You can dent it and live with the dent. You can refuse the word and still have the wood. That refusal is not purity theater. It is a category error avoided. Wellness is a program. Furniture is an object. When the program needs the object to speak, the object is usually the cheaper one.

I have sat in rooms that were full of plants and full of printed grain, and the plants were doing all the living. The furniture was doing what furniture does: holding a glass, taking a scratch, waiting. The better rooms did not narrate the plants. They put a real table under a real window and let Wilson remain a book on a shelf. Fromm, if he is on the same shelf, can keep his meaning too. Love of life is a large claim. A nightstand should not have to carry it.

If you want the benefit Wilson was pointing at, open a window, keep a plant you will water, and buy wood that is wood. If you want the 2020s look, buy the cane and the bouclé and enjoy them as looks. The trouble starts when the hang-tag tells you the look is a treatment. Treatments get revised. Wood, if it is wood, gets oiled. Those are different maintenance schedules. Only one of them comes with a season.

item.title: What Moser and Stickley Ignore
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The arm is one piece of wood that runs from the front post, around your back, and down the other side without a break you can feel. Thos. Moser’s Continuous Arm Chair, designed in 1977, is that line. Tom and Mary Moser had founded the shop in 1972 in a grange in New Gloucester, Maine. The chair is still the piece people can name. The shop moved to Auburn in 1987. Company timeline says they have hand-signed pieces since 1977 [CITE NEEDED against the firm’s own chronology if you want a signature in the wild]. You pick the chair up by the arm and the arm is the structure, not a decoration applied to a structure.

Photo cue: FFF-13a — Thos. Moser Continuous Arm Chair, 1977 design, signed underside or branded mark if present; object on a plain floor, no lifestyle.

Gustav Stickley would have recognized the instinct and argued about the style. He ran The Craftsman from October 1901 to 1916. United Crafts became Craftsman Workshops, Eastwood, Syracuse. He despised “Mission” as a name for the furniture — a sales word, a Spanish fantasy, a label that made the work sound like a revival of something it was not [CITE NEEDED for his exact wording; the dislike is consistent in the secondary literature]. He wanted oak, visible joinery, hardware that looked like it had a job. The magazine taught a reader how to live with that furniture and, not incidentally, how to want it.

He was not alone and he was not the only Stickley. L. & J.G. Stickley — Leopold and John George — set up in Fayetteville, New York, in 1905. Stickley Brothers was in Grand Rapids by 1891. The successor to L. & J.G. still operates in Manlius, New York, which is a continuity most furniture names cannot claim. The brothers disagreed, competed, and sold to overlapping customers. What they shared, when the work was good, was a refusal to hide how a piece went together. What they did not share was a single moral. This is not a sermon about purity. Gustav went bankrupt. Factories cut corners. “Craftsman” became a word other people owned. The useful remainder is a habit: make the joint, finish the wood, do not ask the object to be a year.

Photo cue: FFF-13b — Gustav Stickley oak settle or tabouret, visible tenon or through-mortise, *The Craftsman* page in the background if a public-domain issue is used.

What Moser and the Stickley line ignore is not “fashion” as a human fact. People will always want a new chair. They ignore the apparatus that makes a chair a season. Color-of-the-year is the obvious one. A shop that builds in cherry and walnut does not wait for Pantone. The wood already has a color. You can stain it, and both traditions have stained, but the stain is in service of the board, not in service of a press release. Distressed-on-purpose fashion is the next. Beating a new piece so that it looks inherited is a kind of theater Stickley’s hardware did not need and Moser’s signed chairs do not bother with. The wear arrives. It arrives from use. Pre-distress is a finish schedule for a showroom that will not see use until the customer gets home, and then the fake wear and the real wear argue.

Barn-door hardware as jewelry is a smaller tell, and a louder one. A sliding door on black strap steel became, in the 2010s, a kitchen necklace. The hardware was the point. The door was a prop. A Craftsman hinge, when it was good, was iron because the door was heavy. Moser’s hardware disappears into the job. Logo status is the last ignore. A name burned on the underside is a record. A name on the apron, in brass, facing the dining room, is a handbag. Thos. Moser’s signature, if the timeline is right, is a maker’s mark for the person who turns the chair over. It is not a chest logo for the person across the table.

Retail taught the opposite lessons for a century. Mission became a mall category: dark oak, a clavos nail, a pew that had never been in a church. The 1990s Pottery Barn and the 2000s restoration catalogs sold “artisan” as a stain color. The 2010s sold farmhouse as a barn door and a clock face. None of that is Stickley’s fault, and it is only slightly Moser’s problem. Copies need a name to copy. The original shops keep making the chair. The chair does not have to answer the copy.

Photo cue: FFF-13c — 2010s barn-door kitchen, decorative strap hardware oversized for the slab; real-estate or catalog photograph, for contrast, not admiration.

Status, in the Moser and Stickley worlds, is supposed to be quiet, and sometimes it is not. A signed Continuous Arm in a dining room of a certain kind of New England house is a known object. A Stickley settle in a study is a known object. Collectors pay for labels, for shop marks, for the right stretchers. That market can become as vain as any other. The difference, when there is one, is that the vanity is attached to a joint you can still read. A fake Mission chair with a burned-in name is vanity attached to a burn. Learn the joint. The burn will lie.

The hangover from the fashion versions is in every Habitat for Humanity ReStore: a “Mission” coffee table with a plywood shelf and oak-colored edges, a farmhouse bench whose X-brace is a stencil, a barn door in the garage because the next owner wanted it off the track. The hangover from the real shops is different. It is a chair that needs a new seat rush, a settle that needs a cleaner who understands oil, a table whose top has a cup and can be flattened. Repair is the point. A piece that cannot be repaired was never in this argument.

I am not going to pretend that ignoring a year is a personality. Shops ignore years because their jigs are set up for a chair, not for a collection launch. That is a production fact. It produces, as a side effect, furniture that does not look embarrassed in 1995 or 2015 or 2028. The Continuous Arm is dated 1977 if you know the date. If you do not, it is a chair with a long arm. A Gustav Stickley tabouret is dated if you know The Craftsman. If you do not, it is a small oak table with a visible joint. Dating requires a caption. Aging does not.

Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, is not Moser and is not Stickley, and should not be drafted into a lineage. Its product copy says solid hardwood, no particleboard, no MDF. It also claims Bradley Lumber Co. from 1902, which is company copy until a primary record says otherwise [CITE NEEDED]. The useful neighborliness is only this: a shop that builds in hardwood and does not print the grain is, by habit, ignoring the same apparatus. Color-of-the-year would require them to stain against the board. Distress-on-purpose would require them to damage a top they just flattened. Barn-door jewelry is not a dining table problem. A logo on the apron would be a different business. They can stay a hardwood shop. That is enough of a position.

Photo cue: FFF-13d — underside of a chair, maker’s signature or shop stamp, no face-forward branding; Moser or Stickley, documented.

Stand a Continuous Arm next to a 2016 color-of-the-year side chair from a mall brand. The mall chair will tell you the year even if you sand it. The pigment was the idea. Stand a Stickley settle next to a distressed dining set whose wear was applied with a chain in a factory. The settle’s dents, if it has them, will be in the places a body goes. The factory’s dents will be in the places a camera goes. That is the whole essay, and it is not a moral. It is a map of where the tool hit.

What they ignore, they ignore because looking up would cost them the chair. A year is a short customer. A joint is a long one. Gustav lost the factory anyway. The Mosers built a company that still answers the phone in Maine. L. & J.G.’s successors still build in Manlius. Continuity is not a halo. It is a shop that kept a jig. The jig does not know what Pantone named this year. Good. The year will name itself something else, and the arm will still be one piece.

item.title: Catalog, Showroom, Feed
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The child is lying on the living-room carpet with the Sears Wish Book open to a room that does not exist in the house. A sofa, a lamp, a tree in a tub, a father-shaped blur in a cardigan. The room is a set. The set is for sale in pieces. You could, if the adult cooperated, reconstruct a corner of it. You will remember the corner longer than you remember the chair. That is the catalog’s job: to get the want in before the sit.

Photo cue: FFF-14a — Sears Wish Book interior page, mid-century or 1970s room setting; public-domain or licensed catalog spread, full room in frame.

Sears did not invent the furnished page, but the Wish Book made the furnished page a household object, seasonal, thick enough to sit on. The rooms were typed: colonial, Mediterranean, “modern,” a den with knotty pine. Each type was a kit. The kit taught a family what a room was supposed to contain. Ethan Allen took the next step and put the kit in a gallery — a store that was already a house, so that you walked through the want instead of turning a page. The gallery salesperson could say, as a fact, that this was how the collection lived. You had not sat long. You had walked through a sentence.

Design Within Reach opened in 1999, Rob Forbes’s company, and made a different sentence. It was a catalog and then a shop for furniture that had been, for most Americans, a specifiers’ secret: Herman Miller and the European moderns, sold as if they were available to a person with a credit card and a loft. DWR was, in a real way, a Herman Miller retail catalog channel before it was a mall presence. Herman Miller acquired DWR in 2015. The acquisition is a fact about who owns the picture now. The earlier fact is that Forbes understood the picture as the product’s first life. An Eames lounge in a white room, correctly photographed, is a want that precedes the leather. The leather may disappoint. The photograph rarely does.

IKEA’s catalog — a paper brick that the company treated as a flag — taught a cheaper, more complete version of the same lesson. The rooms were small. The prices were on the page. You could have the whole sentence. The hangover is an apartment of particleboard that looked, in the photograph, like a finished thought. IKEA was honest about the thought being a system. The buyer who wanted the photograph without the allen key was not IKEA’s problem.

Photo cue: FFF-14b — IKEA catalog room, small footprint, price tags visible; dated edition, paper stock obvious.

Wayfair began in 2002 as CSN Stores, a bundle of niche sites, and became a single name later. The picture multiplied. Instead of one Wish Book room or one IKEA kitchen, a search returned a hundred sofas in a hundred identical white rooms, the same houseplant cloned across SKUs. The body still had not met the chair. The chair might arrive in three boxes. The want had already been satisfied and then immediately replaced by the next thumbnail. Instagram and TikTok finished the move from page to feed. A room is now a clip. The clip has a sound. The furniture is a prop that can be tagged. The tag is a link. The link is a cart.

High Point Market, twice a year in High Point, North Carolina, is where a lot of those pictures get their raw material. It is a wholesale taste factory. Buyers walk buildings. Reps stage rooms that will never be lived in. A finish that will be on a thousand retail floors is decided in a showroom that smells like carpet glue and coffee. The shelter magazines used to translate High Point for the public with a lag of months. The feed translated it in a week, then in a day, then in the same afternoon. I will not invent circulation figures for the Wish Book, or unique-visitor counts for Wayfair, or High Point attendance. Those numbers exist in trade reports and they change with the method. The structure does not need them. The picture still goes first.

Status rides the medium. A Wish Book room said: this is what a family owns. An Ethan Allen gallery said: this is what a family aspires to, with a payment plan. DWR said: this is what a person of a certain education sits in. IKEA said: this is what a person of a certain decade can finish in a weekend. Wayfair said: this is what a search returns. The feed says: this is what a stranger’s apartment looks like at 4 p.m. in good light. Each status claim is a picture claim. The chair is asked to live up to a frame.

Photo cue: FFF-14c — High Point Market showroom corridor, staged room through an open door, buyer badge if visible; trade photograph, not a brand ad.

The hangover is a house full of pieces that were bought to complete a picture and then outlived the picture. The Mediterranean suite after the Wish Book went colonial. The gallery collection after Ethan Allen’s next gallery looked different. Walk an older Ethan Allen store even now and you can see the lag: a room that was last year’s page, still fully dressed, waiting for a couple who will sit for thirty seconds and then photograph the fabric. The DWR chair after the loft became a two-bedroom and the dog chose the leather. The IKEA wall after the move, when the cam locks stripped. The Wayfair sectional after the thumbnail’s fabric turned out to be a pile that mats. The feed’s hangover is faster and more personal: a room you copied from a stranger, which dated when the stranger posted the next room. You are left with the objects. The objects were never the point. The point was the frame.

A Saturday in a regional gallery — not Ethan Allen, a cousin with the same script — still runs this way: the salesperson builds a whole room on a clipboard from a catalog spread taped to the podium. The couple nod at the spread, not at the sofa. They have already lived in the picture. The sofa is a delivery problem. That is the hangover in advance. The room arrives. It is smaller. The lamp from the page is back-ordered. The want has nowhere to sit except on what actually came.

What ages, in this system, is a piece that can leave the picture and still be a piece. A walnut table photographed in 1962 in a Wish Book and again in 2014 on a phone is the same table if the top is walnut. A sofa photographed in five catalogs is five sofas. Upholstery is a picture medium. Wood is less so, unless the wood is a print. The feed prefers the print because the print is consistent under a ring light. Consistency is not the same as quality. It is the same as a thumbnail that matches.

A craft shop is almost invisible in the feed unless someone films the shop. Bradley Brand Furniture, Warren, Arkansas, will not be a For You Page unless a customer makes it one. Its copy says solid hardwood, no particleboard or MDF, and dates Bradley Lumber Co. to 1902 as company history pending a primary record [CITE NEEDED]. The contrast is not that a Warren table is above pictures. Everything is pictured now. The contrast is that a table built to be used can survive the death of the picture it was first sold with. A table built to match a picture dies with the picture.

I have watched people sit in a showroom chair for four seconds and then photograph the chair instead. The sit was a formality. The photograph was the decision, to be compared later with other photographs. The body will meet the chair at delivery, when the height is wrong or the seat is deep or the arm hits a hip. By then the want has already been spent. Returns exist. They do not restore the hour you spent inside the picture.

Forbes, if he was honest in 1999, knew that DWR was selling access to a photograph that used to belong to architects. Sears, in any of the thick years, knew it was selling a Christmas morning that included a room. IKEA knew it was selling a plan. The feed does not know it is selling. It is a behavior. The cart is attached afterward, like a hinge on a door that is already swinging.

If you want a chair, sit in one that is not in a picture. If you cannot, sit longer than the clip. The body is still the last to know. That order — picture first, sit later — is the fad. Reverse it and you get a house. Keep it and you get another page.

item.title: What Ages Well
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The table is oak, the top a little proud at one end where a leaf used to live, the finish worn to a pale path between the two chairs that were always used. Someone has put a mason jar of spoons on it. The kitchen around it has been painted four times since 1978. The table has been wiped. That is the whole inheritance. You do not have to love 1970s oak to keep the table. You have to recognize that the top is a board, the boards are joined, and the finish is a film you can cut through without cutting through the idea.

Photo cue: FFF-15a — 1970s solid-oak dining table, worn path in the finish, one leaf seam visible; kitchen light, no styling beyond what is already on the top.

This is a field guide, not a ranking. What ages well in furniture is a short list of mechanical properties dressed up as taste. Solid wood — or a thick veneer over a stable core, honestly described — can be refinished. An honest finish is one you can name: oil, wax, shellac, lacquer, a conversion varnish, even a consumer polyurethane if you know it is there. Repairable joinery is a mortise, a dowel you can drill out, a screw that was not a cam lock, a corner block. The opposite list is also short. Printed grain on a substrate that chips at the edge. A color that was the point of the piece. Upholstery whose cover cannot come off and whose foam is stapled to a frame that will not be worth the recovering bill.

Dining tables age if the top is real. Case goods — dressers, sideboards, chests — age if the drawers run on wood or on a slide you can replace, and if the carcass is not a photograph wrapped around air. Chairs age if the joints can be knocked apart and glued, if the seat is a slip or a pad, if the back is a post and not a molded shell whose only future is a crack. Sofas are a different kingdom. Upholstery is fashion. A sofa can be well made and still be a five-to-twelve-year object for most households, because taste in cloth moves and because bodies ruin cloth. The exception is a frame you will pay to recover, in a shop that still does that work. Most sofas are not that exception. They are the color cycle in foam.

Inherit a 1970s oak table and do this. Do not sand it in the driveway on the first Saturday unless the finish is failing. Clean it. Denatured alcohol on a cloth will tell you if you are dealing with shellac; water will tell you if the top has been living as a bar. If the film is intact and only ugly, you can live with ugly while you decide. If you strip, strip to the wood and stop. 1970s oak is often redder than the present mood. You can tone it down with a stain that has some brown and green in it, or you can leave the red and let the room catch up. Do not “whitewash” it unless you want a 2014 kitchen in 2028. Oil, if the wood can take it, is reversible. A thick consumer polyurethane is a commitment. Either is honest if you choose it on purpose.

Photo cue: FFF-15b — same table mid-clean, finish test patch, no before/after glamour; tools in frame, shop-light truth.

The 1970s oak suite — hutch, table, captain’s chairs — is the hangover people are meanest about, and some of it earned the meanness. A lot of those suites were oak-colored rather than oak, with carved-looking panels that were stamped, and chairs whose stretchers loosened in the first decade. The table, if it is the real member of the family, is still the keeper. Sell or stage the hutch if the hutch is a box of dust and glass doors that rattle. Keep the top that can take a holiday. Status, then, was a matched set. Status now is a mixed room that looks as if someone chose. You can use that. You do not have to sneer at the original buyer. They bought a set because the store sold sets. Sears, Levitz, and a hundred regional floors made the set the default. The default was a picture. The table is what survived the picture.

Printed grain dates on a schedule you can set a clock by. As soon as the print is of a fashion oak — gray, whitewashed, “rustic” with a black wash in the pores — the year is in the paper. You cannot sand a photograph. You can paint it, and then you have a painted photograph. One-year color dates faster: the millennial-pink velvet, the hunter-green wash, the terracotta bouclé that was a clip. Unrepairable upholstery dates in two ways at once. The cloth goes, and the structure will not accept a new cloth at a price a sane person pays. That is why the sofa is the wrong place to spend as if you were buying a table.

A Warren, Arkansas, hardwood island is a different bet than a laminate cart. Bradley Brand Furniture’s product copy says solid hardwood and no particleboard or MDF. The same family of copy places Bradley Lumber Co. at 1902, which is a company claim until a primary record sits beside it [CITE NEEDED]. I am not writing a specification. I am writing a category. An island you can plane is an island you can keep when the cabinets change color. A cart with a printed top and a skinny chrome stem is a cart you will list for twenty dollars because it still rolls. Both objects hold a bowl of fruit. Only one of them is in this field guide.

Photo cue: FFF-15c — solid-hardwood kitchen island, top worn, knife marks; contrasting laminate utility cart in the same frame if you can do it without cruelty.

What ages in a chair is often the least visible part. A post-and-rung chair you can re-glue. A Thonet-style bentwood if the bend has not split. A Moser-type arm if the shop will still talk to you. A 1990s “farmhouse” chair with dowels and glue and a stretch of fiberboard in the seat is a chair you will put at the kid’s table and then not. Hardware ages when it is brass or iron that can be cleaned, not when it is a zinc knob in a trend shape. Barn-door steel on a closet will look like 2016 longer than a plain mortised lockset will look like any year.

Finishes that age are finishes that can dull and be brought back. Oil and wax ask for a hand. Shellac asks for alcohol and skill. Nitrocellulose lacquer, on older case goods, can be melted in and repaired by a finisher who still does that. Conversion varnishes on late-century factory tables are harder; they are also why some of those tables still look “new” in a way that is not quite living. A factory distressing that was meant to look old looks, after ten years of real life, like two times stacked. Stop stacking. If you want old, use the piece.

The hangover from the last twenty years of “fast” case goods is a particular trash-day object: a dresser whose paper surface has lifted at the drawer edge, the white substrate showing like a tooth. Next to it, sometimes, is a 1970s oak table no one wanted to carry. Carry the table. Leave the tooth. I have seen that pair on a curb in the same hour. The street understands this essay. The street is not sentimental about oak. It is sentimental about weight. Weight is a bad proxy, but it is better than a thumbnail.

Retail will keep selling the other list, because the other list photographs. Wayfair, the warehouse clubs, the mall galleries, the feed — they need a new grain and a new color because the old picture has been scrolled past. High Point will mint the grain. A hardwood shop will mint another top. You can buy from both without lying to yourself if you know which purchase is a year and which is a table. A year is allowed. A house that is only years is a catalog that you happen to sleep in.

Inherit the oak table. Wipe it. Decide later about the red. Paint the walls whatever the decade demands. The table will still be there when terracotta is embarrassing, and it was there when harvest gold was proud. That is not virtue. That is a board, kept.

item.title: Hollywood Regency
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The chest is black lacquer, high enough to throw a lamp, the doors a pair of Greek-key panels that catch the light like water. Someone has put a porcelain dog on it. The dog is a little much. The chest can take the dog. That is Hollywood Regency when it is working: a surface that will accept a joke because the surface was built. When it is not working, the same idea is a resin box with a foil key pattern and a palm-print pillow, and the dog looks like the only honest object in the room.

Photo cue: FFF-16a — high-gloss lacquered chest, Greek-key detail, 1940s–50s or a documented later piece in the same construction; object, not a celebrity interior.

Dorothy Draper is the name the hotels keep. She redid the Greenbrier in White Sulphur Springs in the 1940s, after the building had been a wartime hospital, and she put the place back into a kind of American Baroque: cabbage roses, strong color, black and white, a lobby that would photograph. The Tides is the other Draper citation that travels with her name in the brief histories; treat the attribution as something to pin to a dated commission list before you write it in bronze [CITE NEEDED for the exact Tides project and year]. Draper’s point, in the rooms that are still hers, was not “more.” It was scale and nerve. A baroque plaster and a striped chair can be a system. A striped chair alone is a remnant.

William Haines — Billy Haines — came at the same glamour from the studio side. An actor who became a decorator, he did houses for people whose faces were already furniture, and he designed pieces that could stand that company: clean, shiny, a little classical, not cute. Hollywood furniture in his hands was not a prop department leftover. It was a second career with a shop. The 1930s into the 1950s are the years the style still belongs to. Palm motifs, Greek key, high-gloss lacquer, animal print as an accent that knew it was an accent. The studio wanted a room that looked like money in black and white and then in Technicolor. The furniture had to read at thirty feet and also survive a party.

Photo cue: FFF-16b — Dorothy Draper, Greenbrier, 1940s public room, cabbage rose or black-and-white geometry; historic photograph, rights via the hotel archive or a public collection.

Status, then, was proximity to the industry. A Haines sofa in a Bel Air living room said you were in the picture even when you were at home. A Draper hotel lobby said the guest was in a production. That is a specific vanity, and it produced specific objects: lacquer that took labor, brass that had weight, a mirror that was a wall. The hangover, even in the good years, was the cheaper studio-adjacent suite — blond, shiny, a little Spanish, a little French, sold in Los Angeles and then in every city that wanted a taste of the credits. Some of that suite was walnut under the shine. Some of it was already a costume.

The 2000s brought the costume back as a boutique-hotel product. Jonathan Adler, who came up through pottery and then a full interiors line, sold a cheerful, knowing Regency: brass, lacquer colors, a porcelain animal that was in on the joke. Kelly Wearstler put a denser, more mineral version into hotels and houses — pattern on pattern, a Greek key that had been to the gym, animal print that was not shy. The Viceroy and the other Wearstler-era rooms taught a generation of developers what “glamour” looked like in a photograph for a booking site. Adler taught a generation of shops what glamour looked like on a shelf. Both are competent at the joke. The copy that followed them often had only the joke.

Resin is the tell. A well-made lacquered chest is wood, or a stable panel, with film built up and rubbed. It can be repaired by a finisher who still understands rubbing. A resin “lacquer” chest is a molded shine. It chips to a beige wound. Greek key in inlay or in a painted band is a drawing on a surface that exists. Greek key in a decal or a printed PVC is a drawing on a drawing. Palm motifs in a good textile are leaves someone decided to stylize. Palm motifs on a peel-and-stick mural behind a gold sofa are a vacation the room cannot take. Animal print on a pillow is a tradition. Animal print on every vertical surface is a costume department that lost the lead actor.

Photo cue: FFF-16c — 2000s boutique-hotel lobby, Wearstler-era or after, Greek key and animal print in one frame; booking photograph or published interior, rights dependent.

Retail spread the revival through Jonathan Adler stores, through Wearstler’s books and the hotel copycats, through Restoration Hardware’s shinier years, through every “glam” collection at the mall that put a crystal finial on a lamp and called it Hollywood. High Point minted brass-and-black suites that had never been near a studio. Wayfair still returns a hundred “Hollywood Regency” nightstands, most of them a cam-lock box with a chrome handle. The name, like Mission, like Tuscany, like farmhouse, became a filter. Filters do not age. They date.

What ages is the well-made lacquered chest, the brass that can be polished, the chair whose show-wood is actually wood, the mirror that is heavy enough to need two people. Those objects can leave Bel Air and live in a smaller room if you let them be furniture instead of a set. What dates is the resin version, the palm that came in a roll, the faux-shagreen that is a vinyl, the chandelier that is a photograph of a chandelier. The 2000s boutique-hotel copy dates fastest when it was all accent: no quiet surface, no place for the eye to stop, a room that required the ice machine down the hall to make sense.

A Greenbrier corridor and a suburban dining room can use the same black-and-white stripe. The corridor has the stripe as a beat in a larger system. The dining room has the stripe as the system. Draper can survive the first. She cannot be blamed for the second. Haines cannot be blamed for the nightstand with the Greek-key sticker. Adler and Wearstler can be blamed only for being good enough to copy. Copy is the fad mechanism. It always has been.

Photo cue: FFF-16d — resin “lacquer” nightstand, chip on a corner showing substrate, Greek-key decal lifting; object photography, hangover evidence.

A hardwood shop will not, as a rule, make Hollywood Regency, and should not be asked to as a personality test. Bradley Brand Furniture in Warren, Arkansas, talks solid hardwood and no particleboard or MDF in its product language; it also attaches Bradley Lumber Co. to 1902 in that language, which stays company copy until a primary record confirms it [CITE NEEDED]. The useful contrast is construction, not taste. Lacquer over a stable hardwood chest is a finish on furniture. Shine over a resin box is a finish on a product cycle. You can want the shine. You should know which substrate you are shining.

Animal print, while we are here, ages only as an accent and only if the cloth is cloth. A 1950s leopard chair in a real hide or a real textile, kept as one object in a quiet room, still has nerve. A 2018 leopard rug under a gold coffee table under a palm mural is a year. High-gloss ages if someone will rub it out when it dulls. High-gloss dates if it was never a film, only a plastic. Greek key ages if it is drawn once, at a scale that fits the piece. It dates if it is a border on everything, including the wastebasket.

The studio rooms were sets, and they knew it. That self-knowledge is what the good pieces kept: a chest that could walk out of the set and still be a chest. The boutique-hotel rooms of the 2000s were sets that wanted to be booked. The booking photograph is a hard master. It wants the palm, the key, the print, the shine, in one frame, because the guest is scrolling. Furniture that exists to satisfy a scroll is already in the same trouble as furniture that existed to satisfy a Wish Book page. The body arrives later, with a suitcase, and sits on a bench that was specified as a stripe.

Keep the lacquered chest if the doors still close and the film can be saved. Give the resin key-pattern box to the next production. Hollywood Regency, when it was a shop and a hotel and a decorator with a drawing account, made objects that could carry a porcelain dog. The fad version makes the dog do all the work. The dog is tired. Let the chest work. If there is no chest — if there is only a palm and a shine — you are not in the 1940s. You are in a listing. Listings refresh. Lacquer, if it is lacquer, can be rubbed again.

item.title: The Wheat-Sheaf Chair Was a Ticket Out of Oak
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The chair in the corner has a wheat sheaf carved into the crest rail, the ears of grain fanned like a badge, and a rush seat that has gone the color of old straw. Someone sat here for decades. The rush has a hip-shaped dish in it. The cherry — or the stain that wanted to be cherry — has a wear stripe on the front stretcher where a shoe scuffed every supper. This is the object that survived the American Country French binge, and it is not the gold-leaf console that came in the same catalog spread.

Photo cue: FFF-17a — A rush-seat side chair with a carved wheat-sheaf crest, wear on the front stretcher, no gilt.

What Americans called French Provincial in the 1980s and 1990s was not a province. It was a mood purchased against another mood. The decade before had sold oak Mediterranean: dark, heavy, scrolled, the dining set that looked as if it had been dragged from a villa that never existed. Provincial was the vacation. Lighter wood. Distressed cherry. Toile at the window. A little farmhouse, a little château, nothing that required you to know which. Laura Ashley had already trained the eye on small florals and cottage romance; Country French was the same hunger pointed at Provence instead of the Cotswolds. You could buy it at Ethan Allen. You could buy it at a mall gallery that smelled of potpourri. You could buy a cheaper cousin at a chain that had just discovered the word distressed.

Pierre Deux made the look feel imported. The shop opened in Greenwich Village in 1967, founded by Pierre Moulin and Pierre LeVec — the two Pierres who gave the firm its name (Los Angeles Times, 17 Feb. 1990; Moulin’s New York Times obituary, 19 Oct. 1999). Later hangtags sometimes invent a “J. Popin”; the Times papers name LeVec [CITE NEEDED if a third founder appears on a primary document]. They sold Provençal cottons, glazed tile, and antique armoires that had actually stood in French rooms. The fabrics did the heavy lifting. Souleiado-adjacent prints — paisleys, sprigs, busy little grounds that read as “south of France” from across a showroom — sold harder than the case goods. In the mid-1980s they put a book on the American coffee table: Pierre Deux’s French Country: A Style and Source Book, with Moulin, LeVec, and Linda Dannenberg, Clarkson Potter (trade listings split 1984 and 1989 — [CITE NEEDED] on the first-edition year). Hundreds of photographs of ochre farmhouses and rush banquettes. A directory of sources. A catalog disguised as a region.

By 1990 Pierre Deux was already doing what every successful importer does: less pricey versions of the same dream (LAT, same 1990 piece). That is the hinge. The antique rush-seat banquette is one object. The American factory chair with a wheat-sheaf stamp and a cherry glaze is another. Both got called provincial. Only one of them had been a chair in France.

Ethan Allen’s French collections — Country French, French Country, the names slid — put the look in rooms that already had a wing chair and a brass lamp. The company already meant “traditional” you could finance. The French suites were the same contract: a table, four or six chairs, a sideboard, maybe a china cabinet with a wheat carving, all in a distressed finish that suggested age without requiring it. The rush seats, when they were real rush, were the honest part. The rest was theater. Distressed cherry is a finish, not a biography. A belt sander and a glaze can put a century on a rail that left the factory last Tuesday.

Toile de Jouy did the wall and the pillow. Pastoral scenes in a single color on cream: shepherds, ruins, a river that never muddies. Brunschwig & Fils and the old document houses had sold the real stuff for years. The 1980s suburban version arrived as a border, a duvet, a wallpaper sample book at the paint store. Pair it with a ladder-back chair and you had “French” without speaking any. Laura Ashley’s English cottage and Pierre Deux’s Provence sat on the same American sofa more often than either firm would have liked. The customer was not choosing a nation. She was choosing not-oak.

Status was the point, and it was a soft status. Mediterranean oak had been a dinner-party flex: I have a dining room, it is dark, it is complete. Country French said something more flattering. I have been to the countryside. I know about rush. I own a sheaf of wheat in wood. It was leisure coded as simplicity, which is the oldest rich trick in the furniture book. A real Provençal farmhouse chair is simple because a farmer sat on it. An American provincial suite is simple because the catalog said Informal elegance in a serif font. The wheat sheaf is agricultural heraldry for people whose wheat arrives as bread.

Walk a 1992 model home in a Sun Belt subdivision and you can still smell it. Cherry stain on poplar or worse. Gold-leaf highlights on a carved apron that was pressed, not cut. A mirror with a “Provençal” pediment and a factory gilt that flakes if you look at it. The table has a parquet top printed on a veneer so thin a hot casserole leaves a ghost. Under the distressed cherry, if you nick it, you find a core that is not cherry. Sometimes it is not even wood in the old sense.

Photo cue: FFF-17b — A 1980s–90s American “French” dining suite in a catalog spread: distressed cherry, gilt highlights, toile swatch in the corner. Rights: period catalog, not Pierre Deux antiques.

The hangover is specific. Gold-leaf flourishes on MDF. That is the sentence that should have stopped a purchase and did not. Medium-density fiberboard takes a router profile and a metallic paint the way a cake takes icing. It photographs. It does not take a second life. When the gilt goes dull and the corners swell from a humid summer, there is no repair that is not a confession. You can strip a solid cherry apron and start over. You cannot un-swell a particle core and call it a farmhouse.

Facebook Marketplace is full of these suites now, priced for the cost of a truck and a Saturday. The wheat-sheaf chairs still find sitters if the rush is intact. The gilt console does not. It looks like 1994, which is a compliment only if you are writing this series. The toile wallpaper got painted. The ladder-backs got a milk-paint experiment in 2011 and another in 2018. Provincial, as a whole-house idea, dated the way a vacation slides: you come home, the souvenir is still on the mantel, and you cannot remember why you needed the whole set.

What survived is narrower and better. A real rush-seat chair. Not a paper-rush lookalike, not a foam pad printed with a weave. Rush — cattail, bulrush, the twisted fiber that has been a seat in Europe for centuries — can be rewoven. The skill is not common on every Main Street, but it exists. A caner or a seater who still takes work will strip the old stuff, soak the new, and put a seat back on a frame that was built to take it. That frame matters. If the posts are solid hardwood, if the joinery is mortise and tenon or at least a peg that is wood, the chair is a chair again. If the frame is a dowel-and-glue carcass with a decorative crest glued to a panel, recaning is a kindness the object does not deserve.

A shop that still works in solid hardwood, the way Bradley Brand Furniture in Warren, Arkansas, describes its own line — Bradley Lumber back to 1902, in the company’s copy; no particleboard — would have made the wheat-sheaf chair as a chair, not as a souvenir of a catalog. Cherry that is cherry. A seat that can be replaced. No metallic paint on a pressed flourish. That is not a sales pitch. It is a refusal. The provincial fad needed the flourish because the flourish was how you proved the set was “French” from the parking lot. A hardwood shop that will not sell a particle core has nothing to hide under gilt, so it tends not to apply the gilt.

I have seen more of these chairs at estate sales than I have seen of the armoires Pierre Deux actually imported. The armoires went to people who knew what they had, or to dealers who still do. The wheat-sheaf set went to the next suburb and then to the Habitat ReStore. That is not a moral ranking of the buyers. It is a material ranking of the objects. One of them was built as furniture. The other was built as a finish.

Ethan Allen’s better French pieces — the ones in solid maple or cherry, not the promotional veneers — still sit in dining rooms that have otherwise gone white-oak modern. They look slightly costume, like a good actor in the wrong play, but they work. You eat on them. You do not apologize for a rush seat. What you apologize for, if you apologize at all, is the matching gilt mirror you finally took to the curb.

Country French, as America bought it, was a correction with a costume department. Provence-by-way-of-Greenwich-Village was a real shop and a real book. The mall version was a stain and a sheaf. Laura Ashley adjacent, Pierre Deux adjacent, Ethan Allen as the respectable middle. The hangover is the gold leaf on the fiberboard in a guest room nobody uses. The thing that ages is the rush-seat chair with the worn stretcher, which never needed to be French to be a chair.

Photo cue: FFF-17c — Close on a recaned or original rush seat, showing the twist of the fiber and the hardwood seat rails. No gilt in the frame.

Craft, here, is not a mood. It is whether the crest is carved from the same wood as the post, or applied like a brooch. It is whether “distressed” is a century of elbows or a factory glaze. It is whether the seat can be sat into and then remade. Provincial style will come back; it already has, in quieter paint and less gold, every time a designer wants “collected Europe” without buying Europe. The test is the same as it was in 1988. Pick up the chair. Look at the underside of the seat rails. If you find a stamped sheaf and a hollow core, you have bought a year. If you find rush on hardwood, you have bought a seat.

item.title: Howling Coyote, Bleached Pine, and the Mall Desert
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The coyote is howling on a kitchen wall in Ohio. He is black, cut from sheet metal or printed on a plaque, head tipped back, a little bandanna implied if not painted. Under him: a bleached-pine dinette, terracotta tile glued to a tabletop that is not stone, and a runner with a stepped diamond that wants you to think of a chief’s blanket. The house has vinyl siding. There is no mesa. This is the 1980s Southwestern boom as it actually arrived — not in Santa Fe, but in a subdivision that had never seen a viga until a decorator ordered one in foam and whitewash.

Photo cue: FFF-18a — Period kitchen or sunroom: bleached pine, terracotta-tile table, howling-coyote silhouette. Note the non-desert suburb if the slide shows one.

Santa Fe had a real boom. The city’s adobe and pueblo revival architecture, the galleries on Canyon Road, the tourist trade that thickened in the 1970s and 1980s — that is a place with a climate and a history. What furniture stores sold as “Southwestern” was a climate of the mind. Bleached pine. Washed finishes that made new wood look sunstruck. Terracotta, or a glaze that impersonated it, on cocktail tables and lamp bases. Pastel Navajo-ish patterns on upholstery and area rugs: pink, turquoise, sand, a geometric that had been through the mill and come out mall.

The last point needs a hard line. Diné weaving — Navajo weaving, if you use the older English name and mean the same people — is not a fad. It is a textile tradition with named regions, named weavers, wool, and a market that has been distorted by traders and tourists for more than a century. A Two Grey Hills rug is not a throw pillow from Pier 1. A Germantown eye-dazzler from the late nineteenth century is not a pastel diamond printed on olefin. This essay is about the printed cousin: the pattern as atmosphere, sold by the yard, unconnected to a loom in the Navajo Nation. Flattening Native work into a 1986 color story is how the fad thought. It is not how the work should be written.

Ralph Lauren understood the difference between a place and a collection, and sold the collection. In 1981 he put a Santa Fe line on the runway: Native-inspired prints, frontier clothes, prairie dust in a New York show (Vanity Fair’s Lauren chronology, 2012). In 1983 Ralph Lauren Home opened with Log Cabin, Thoroughbred, New England, and Jamaica — American rooms as wardrobes (company history; October 1983 home catalog). Southwestern and desert motifs kept returning in apparel and, later, in home lines that wore names like Desert Modern [CITE NEEDED on the first year a Desert-titled furniture suite shipped]. Canyon Road, much later, made the West a Milan installation. None of this is ethnography. It is fashion. Fashion is allowed to borrow a sky. It is not allowed to call the borrowing a people.

The mall did not bother with Lauren’s restraint. Pier 1 Imports, the furniture wings of department stores, the “Santa Fe” boutique in a strip center: cactus lamps with ceramic arms, howling coyotes in every register from cast iron to refrigerator magnet, whitewashed beams stuck to a flat ceiling in Plano or Indianapolis. Vigas — the round roof beams of adobe construction — are structural in New Mexico. In a 1988 great room in a non-desert suburb they were half-round foam or pine, painted chalk, nailed up as jewelry. The room said ranch. The HVAC said Ohio.

Kitsch has a face here, and the face is the coyote. The howling coyote silhouette became a Southwestern hieroglyph the way the flamingo became Florida: instantly readable, cheap to stamp, slightly comic even when the owner was earnest. I will not invent an artist of record for the first yard-art coyote; the motif spread faster than attribution [CITE NEEDED for a first commercial designer]. What matters is saturation. Once the coyote is on the mailbox, the switch plate, and the toilet-tank cover, the furniture has to keep up. Bleached pine armoires with punched-tin panels. Chairs with ladder backs and a “distressed” wash in peach or aqua. A sofa in a pastel blanket stripe that pills in a year. The terracotta-tile table — tiles set in a wood frame, grout that darkens, edges that chip — was the coffee-table version of a hacienda floor, scaled for a wall-to-wall carpet.

Status was vacation and earthiness at once. You were not the brass-and-glass person anymore. You were not the Mediterranean-oak person. You had discovered the West, or the catalog had discovered it for you, and the West in 1985 meant texture: rough wood, clay, a textile that looked handmade if you squinted. It was a moral upgrade that required no politics. Adobe-colored walls, a kiva fireplace that never saw a pueblo, a pot that looked like Acoma until you turned it over and found a sticker from a gift shop in Albuquerque Airport — or, more often, from a factory that had never been to New Mexico. The owner got to feel closer to land. The land was a finish.

Photo cue: FFF-18b — Ralph Lauren Santa Fe–era fashion or Home catalog page beside a mall “Southwestern” dinette. Caption must say fashion, not Diné weaving.

Retail had a ladder. At the top: actual Navajo textiles, Spanish colonial furniture from New Mexican makers, the kind of carved pine chest that a Santa Fe dealer would stand behind. In the middle: Lauren, and the better department-store interpretations — solid pine, real leather, a blanket that at least was wool. At the bottom: the pastel suite, the foam viga, the cactus lamp whose “pottery” is slip-cast and whose shade is a parchment printed with Kokopelli. Kokopelli, the humpbacked flute player, got the same treatment as the coyote. A figure with a long ceremonial and commercial history became a drawer pull. That is not appreciation. That is clip art.

The 1990s did not kill the look so much as bleach it further, then walk away. By the time Tuscan kitchens and buttery yellow walls took the magazine covers, Southwestern pastel already looked like a time stamp. The pine went from sun-bleached to just cheap. The punched tin dented. The tile tables lost grout in the dishwasher era, when nobody wanted a table you could not wipe with one rag. Whitewashed beams, once a romance, read as a theme restaurant. People painted the pine dark or white, depending on which recovery they were in. Some of the better solid-pine pieces survived that paint and can be stripped. The pastel stain on a soft wood is harder to undo than the catalog promised. Bleach and pigment go deep when the mill wants them to.

The hangover is standing in a Habitat for Humanity ReStore, usually along the back wall with the other case goods that did not sell online. A pastel pine armoire. Peach or washed turquoise, maybe a sun motif routed into a door, maybe tin that has oxidized into a color the designer did not choose. It is too big to ignore and too dated to place. Someone will buy it for a cabin, or for a kid’s room, or to paint navy. The coyote plaques go in a different bin. They have become joke objects, which is a kind of honesty the armoire has not earned yet.

What dates is the costume applied to a room that is not in the desert: the fake viga, the pastel Navajo-ish print, the coyote as punctuation. What ages is more stubborn and less theatrical. A solid pine or hardwood chest that can take a new finish. A wool blanket that was woven as a blanket, not printed as a vibe — and if it is Diné work, it ages as art and as utility, not as a fad, and it should be named that way. A terracotta floor tile that is actually fired clay, set in a house that can carry the weight, will outlast the tile-top table. The table was always a souvenir.

Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, does not sell a Santa Fe collection. The company’s own copy still points at Bradley Lumber, 1902, and at solid hardwood without particleboard. That is useful here only as a contrast in material, not as a Western fantasy. Bleached pine from a 1987 suite and a hardwood case built to be refinished are both wood until you ask them to live a second life. One of them was stained to look like weather. The other can take weather, or a darker stain, or a repair at the corner where the kid hit it with a tricycle. A punched-tin panel on MDF is a picture of the Southwest. A hardwood door is a door.

I have stood under more fake vigas than real ones. The fake ones are lighter. That is the tell, and it is also the joke. You can have a desert in a climate-controlled mall, but you cannot have the weight. The 1980s Southwestern room wanted the weight of adobe and the ease of a credit application. It got a wash, a silhouette, and a pattern that had been through so many printers it no longer pointed at a weaver.

If you are keeping one object from that binge, keep the one that is wood all the way through and has no coyote on it. Let the Diné textile, if you are lucky enough to own one, sit outside this essay’s fad entirely. It was never asking to be a dinette. The pastel pine armoire can go to the Habitat store. It has already done the work of telling a decade. The decade is over. The howl, on the Ohio kitchen wall, can come down whenever you are ready to hear the quiet.

Photo cue: FFF-18c — A Habitat ReStore or thrift aisle: pastel pine armoire, punched tin, sun motif. No Native textile used as a prop for kitsch.
