item.title: Old Furniture Got a Ticker
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The listing said “Eames lounge, Herman Miller, original,” and the photographs said otherwise. The rosewood was a print. The seat angle was a cousin, not a sibling. The ottoman sat a little too high. In the comments — there are always comments — someone typed the serial-number lecture and someone else typed “Eames style is fine if you’re honest.” The price sat between a real one and a joke. That interval is the market now.

Vintage furniture used to be how you avoided the catalog. Estate sales, the uncle’s basement, a church rummage, Craigslist when Craigslist was still a city wall. You bought a thing because it was there and it was cheaper than new, or because it was better than new and the person selling it did not know. The information was uneven. That unevenness was the last bargain in American furniture.

Then the information evened out. 1stDibs, founded in 2000 by Michael Bruno, turned the Paris flea-market walk into a remote catalog with dealer names and asking prices that assumed a shipping crate. [CITE NEEDED on the founding month and the first-year inventory mix.] Chairish, 2013, made the same bet for a less formal room: the sofa your neighbor was tired of, the lamp a decorator was rotating out, a commission for the platform. [CITE NEEDED on the Chairish launch details if you print them.] Craigslist kept the ugly fluorescent version of the trade. Instagram added the handsome dealer who shoots a teak sideboard on terrazzo and will not tell you the reserve.

Photo cue: FFF-37a — A 1stDibs or Chairish-type product page (screenshot with UI chrome cropped if rights require) next to a handwritten estate-sale tag on a real teak dresser. Rights: your own photographs of a sale; marketplace UI only with permission or as a drawn schematic.

Midcentury modern became a ticker. Teak peaked in the public eye around 2014, when every design feed decided a Danish sideboard was the adult purchase and the word Danish started appearing on American walnut. Marble and brass had a loud year around 2018: the tulip table, the drinks cart, the lamp that looked like a hotel in 1972. Mediterranean oak — the heavier, browner, carved or simply thick European look — is the maybe-next, the one dealers are already testing in captions. I am dating those years the way a shop dates a finish: by what walked in the door and what the asking prices did, not by a study. If you have a better peak, write it in the margin.

The authentic Eames lounge — Charles and Ray Eames, Herman Miller, 1956 — is a known object with a known fake. Shock mounts, a shell, a contract with a factory. There are serials, replacement parts, and a service culture. “Eames style” is a legally careful phrase that means: we took the silhouette and none of the liability. Both objects sit on the same apps now. The apps are not a museum. They are a mall with better lighting. A new buyer learns the difference the expensive way, or learns it from a forum, or never learns it and lives with a chair that looks right in a photograph from six feet.

Auction houses still do the old work: catalogs with condition reports, specialists who will tell you the marquetry is later, a hammer price that is public. Sotheby’s, Christie’s, Wright, Rago, the regional rooms that still print an estimate and a provenance paragraph — they are not saints. They have sold copies. They have also published the copy as a copy, which is more than a caption usually does. The Instagram dealer does a different work: narrative, scarcity, a story about a Palm Springs estate that may or may not have a bill of sale behind it. Some dealers are straight. Some are inventing provenance the way a catalog invents lifestyle. The feed rewards the story. The auction house, at its best, rewards the object. At its worst it rewards the same story with a lot number.

The ticker has a few documented beats if you watched asking prices instead of mood boards. 2012 to 2015, teak and the broader “Danish” tag: sideboards, sewing tables pressed into consoles, chairs with paper-cord seats that were either original or a weekend re-wrap. 2016 to 2019, marble tops and brass stems, the tulip and the drinks cart, anything that could sit under a globe pendant and look like a hotel bar. 2020 to 2022, the pale wood and the blob chair, which is another essay, and a run on anything labeled “organic modern.” Mediterranean oak — heavier, browner, a carved or simply thick European case — is the maybe-next. Dealers are already writing “European oak” under American pieces that are only oak. The caption is doing the fashion. The wood is doing what wood does.

Photo cue: FFF-37b — An authentic marked Herman Miller or Knoll piece (museum or documented private) beside an unmarked “style” piece of the same silhouette. Caption the difference in the wood, the joint, the hardware. Rights: museum or owner permission.

Buying used was the anti-fad. You were supposed to be opting out of the circular, the package, the West Elm kit, the white slipcover. You were supposed to be taking the thing that had already survived a fashion and would survive yours. Then the fashion moved onto the used object. A teak dresser is not safer from dating than a new dresser if you bought it because 2014 told you teak was the year. You paid a fashion premium for an old thing. The old thing is still old. The premium is what dates you.

I have watched people flip a chair in eighteen months because the marble-brass year ended and the chair was chrome. The chair did not change. The caption did. That is a fashion market with inventory that happens to have been built in 1968. The build year is not a moral shield. It is a material fact. Material facts are why used furniture is still worth buying. Fashion is why it is suddenly expensive.

Estate sales remain the least fashionable door, which is why they still occasionally work. You walk a house in a morning, you look at the underside, you open a drawer, you smell whether the “teak” is teak. You pay the family or the company running the sale. You do not pay a dealer’s narrative. You also buy a lot of junk, and you need a truck, and you need to know what a dovetail looks like when it was cut by a machine in 1978 versus a bench in 1930. The knowledge is the discount. Platforms flattened the discount by teaching everyone the words. They did not flatten the ability to look at a joint.

Bradley Brand Furniture, in Warren, Arkansas, sells new hardwood and says so: company copy claims a 1902 lumber line and a refusal of particleboard. [CITE NEEDED.] That shop is not a vintage dealer. The useful contrast is still the same sentence. A solid case piece, new or old, has a next life: a refinish, a hardware change, a drawer repair. A fashion object — new printed grain or old plywood that was already tired — has a next listing. If you are buying used as an anti-fad, buy the next life. If you are buying used as a fashion year, admit the year. The admission is cheaper than the story.

What ages: a marked piece from a factory that still exists or is well documented; an unmarked piece whose wood and joints can take another century of ordinary use; a table whose top is thick enough to plane. What dates: the “Eames style” bought at peak caption; the Mediterranean-oak sideboard purchased because a reel said Europe was back; the entire matching vintage kit assembled from three apps in a weekend to look like an apartment that had been inherited. Inheritance takes longer than a weekend.

The hangover is already in storage units. Teak that missed the 2014 window and now looks like brown furniture again. Brass-and-marble carts that photograph as 2018. Blond wood that had a year and then lost it. None of that wood asked to be a ticker. People did that. People can stop.

Craigslist and the estate sale still punish haste and reward a truck. That is their remaining virtue. 1stDibs and Chairish punish ignorance and reward a shipping budget. That is their remaining vice, or their business, depending on whether you needed the crate. Both can get you a good object. Both can get you a silhouette with a story stapled to it. The anti-fad that became a fad is not “buying old.” Buying old is ordinary. The fad is buying old on time, in the year the caption named, at the price the caption taught. A teak dresser bought in 1998 because it was thirty dollars is not a fashion victim. A teak dresser bought in 2014 because a feed said Denmark is how you grow up — that dresser is a subscription. The wood cannot tell the difference. Your receipt can.

A used chair is still the right purchase when the chair is a chair. It becomes the wrong one when it is a share. The oldest furniture advice in this series is also the least fashionable: open the drawer. Look at the back. Sit in it. If the listing’s paragraph is longer than the time you spent looking, you are buying the paragraph.

item.title: The Wall Was the Fashion
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The dining room had been new in 1998. By 2003 it was old Rome. Someone had rag-rolled a terracotta glaze over builder beige, dragged a darker umber through the corners, and stamped a few “fleur-de-lis” with a store-bought stencil that still had the plastic flash on the edges. The table below it was a softwood box with a painted faux-bois top: knots where no tree had put them, a grain that ran in two directions and met in a shrug. Candlelight was supposed to forgive all of it. Fluorescent lunch did not.

Faux finish is older than the 1990s. Venetian plaster, in competent hands, is a lime craft with a long Italian life. Graining — faux bois — is a nineteenth-century trade skill used to make pine look like oak when oak was the expensive word. Marbling on wood and plaster is in every old civic building that could not afford the stone. The 1990s did not invent the lie. The 1990s sold the lie as a weekend kit, in a tub, with a sea sponge still in the shrink-wrap.

Photo cue: FFF-38a — A 1990s–early-2000s dining room: rag-rolled or sponged walls in gold-terracotta, a dark wood table, a wrought-iron chandelier. Rights: period interior photograph or a documented Trading Spaces set still, licensed.

Home centers put the kits at eye level. Sponge painting: dab a glaze so the wall looks mottled, “old world,” or simply busy enough that you cannot see the tape joints. Rag-rolling: a bunched cloth rolled through glaze to make a pattern that read as fabric if you wanted it to. Color washing. Strié. The Venetian plaster kit that was not lime and not Venetian, just a joint compound with dust in it and a trowel the size of a paperback. Tuscan glaze — the marketing name that did the most damage — turned new drywall into a restaurant in a strip center: gold, rust, a smear of brown in the corners to imply soot from a hearth that had never existed.

Trading Spaces ran on TLC from 2000 to 2008 and made the weekend into television. [CITE NEEDED on exact premiere date if you print the day; the years are the broadcast run people remember.] Two sets of neighbors, two rooms, a designer, a carpenter, a clock. Paige Davis hosted. Designers including Hildi Santo-Tomas, Vern Yip, Laurie Hickson-Smith, and others treated walls as the cheapest way to get a gasp. Hay on the walls. A mural. A color that would not have survived a sample board. The show was not the origin of faux finish. It was the amplifier. A nation watched a room become a theme in two days and then went to the hardware store.

I am not blaming the carpenters. The carpenters were often the only people on that set building something that could be used after the theme died. The designers were doing what television pays for: a reveal. A reveal needs a surface. Paint is fast. Furniture is slow. So the fashion moved onto the wall and onto the cheap table that could be made to look like a Tuscan farm table before Saturday night.

Faux bois on cheap tables is the furniture version of the same instinct. A printed grain or a painted grain over a softwood or a composite. The “driftwood” finish that was a chain of dirty-white strokes. The “antique” crackle kit, a two-part varnish that made a new coffee table look like it had been in a barn that never existed. The finish was the entire fashion. Under it, the substrate was whatever the factory had: pine, MDF, particleboard, a veneer thin enough to sand through in one angry afternoon.

Photo cue: FFF-38b — Detail of faux bois on a tabletop: painted knots, grain that does not match the edge. Beside it, a real oak or walnut edge with pores you can feel. Rights: original detail photography.

Here is the only distinction that matters after the fashion leaves. What can be sanded off, and what is the substrate. A hardwood top can lose a bad stain. A bad glaze, a bad crackle, a bad “walnut” that was a can. You take it to bare wood, you accept the loss of thickness, you put on a quieter finish. The object remains an object. A paper veneer cannot do that. Sand the fashion off a paper veneer and you have paper. Sand a vinyl wrap and you have the wrap’s glue. Sand a painted MDF and you have a fuzzy gray board that will never take a stain like wood because it is not wood.

Walls are the same grammar. A rag-roll on drywall can be primed and painted. It is work, and the ridges of glaze can telegraph, but the wall is still a wall. A foam “stone” veneer glued to the same drywall is a different problem. A Venetian plaster kit that was really joint compound may chip in sheets. The Tuscan corner-smear, if it was just glaze, dies under two coats of primer. If someone embedded grit or used an oil glaze without sealing, you learn about it when the new paint crawls. The 1990s liked oil glazes. The 1990s did not like reading the back of the can.

Status, for a while, was Mediterranean. Not the Mediterranean. A restaurant idea of Tuscany that had passed through a cable channel and a gallon of Ralph Lauren-type specialty finish. [CITE NEEDED before naming a specific Ralph Lauren paint SKU; the broader “suede” and “antique” specialty lines were everywhere.] A sponged gold dining room said you had been to Italy in your mind. A crackle-finished armoire said you had ancestors. The ancestors were a kit from a craft aisle.

The hangover is still on the market. Houses listed as “updated 2004” with one dining room that nobody had the energy to prime. Faux-bois tables at thrift stores, priced as wood by someone who did not flip them over. Trading Spaces rooms that became punchlines, then became nostalgia, then became punchlines again. Some of the plaster work was competent. Competence does not photograph differently from the kit at listing-photo resolution. Buyers paint everything white and call it a reset. Sometimes it is. Sometimes the grit is still there, under the white, waiting for a raking light.

Bradley Brand Furniture, Warren, Arkansas, sells hardwood case goods and states a no-particleboard rule in its own copy, with a lumber date of 1902. [CITE NEEDED.] A shop like that cannot help you rag-roll a wall, and should not. What it can do — what any bench that still sands — is refuse the idea that the surface is the whole object. A finish is a coat. A top is a thickness. If the fashion lives only in the coat, you can change your mind. If the fashion is the board, you are stuck with the year.

I have seen a 1990s oak table, real oak, that someone had crackle-finished in a fit of cable courage. Ugly as a theme restaurant. Under the crackle, a top that still had a quarter-inch to give. Two days of stripping and a dull oil later, it was a table again. I have also seen a “farm table” from the same year whose top was a printed paper on particle core. Water had lifted a corner. There was no next finish. There was a landfill, or a garage, or a listing that used the word rustic.

What ages: the substrate that can take the next honest coat — plaster that is actually plaster, wood that is actually wood, a wall that was only painted. What dates: the complete Tuscan kit, the sponge that is still visible in the powder room, the faux-bois dining set that matches the wall because both were bought from the same idea of Italy. The idea was a surface. Surfaces move.

Trading Spaces ended its first run in 2008. The rooms did not end. They waited, under a coat of rental beige, or they sat in a listing photograph while a realtor cropped tight on the kitchen. Fashion that lives on a wall is supposed to be easy to undo. That was the sales pitch of the kit. The pitch was half true. Paint is easy. A theme is not. A theme gets into the furniture, the iron chandelier, the grape motif on the backsplash, the table that was grained to match a villa. Pull one thread and the decade is still sitting in the chairs.

If you are standing in a sponged room now, do the wall last. Flip the table first. If the top is wood, you have a project. If the top is a picture of wood, you have a date stamp. The date stamp was the product. The villa was never included.

item.title: The Knob Is a Calendar
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
Open a junk drawer in a house that has been owned twice and you will find the last decade in metal. A polished-brass rosette from 1987. A satin-nickel bar from 2001. An oil-rubbed bronze orb that still has the fake wear in the crevices, applied at the factory. A brushed-gold cup pull that matched a 2014 faucet. A matte-black hex knob, 2018, the screw still in it. Someone kept them because hardware feels like money even when it cost four dollars. Someone will put one of them back on a cabinet “temporarily.” Temporarily is how rooms get dated.

Kitchen and furniture hardware is the fastest metal cycle in the house. Cabinets are expensive to replace. Knobs are not. So the industry sells you a new year without selling you a new box. The wood — or the MDF that is pretending to be wood — stays. The jewelry changes. If you want to know what year a listing photograph was staged, do not look at the sofa first. Look at the pulls.

Photo cue: FFF-39a — A tray of detached knobs and pulls arranged by finish: polished brass, chrome, satin nickel, oil-rubbed bronze, brushed gold, matte black, unlacquered brass. Rights: original still-life; include a ruler or a 1980s cabinet door as scale.

Polished brass owned the 1980s. Bright, yellow, lacquered so it would not spot, matching the faucet, the towel bar, the entry lamp, the chandelier that looked like a brass bouquet. The lacquer yellowed. The yellowing was blamed on the brass, which is a metal that would have been fine if anyone had been willing to polish it. Instead the 1990s called brass “dated” and ran to chrome and satin nickel. Nickel photographed as clean. Chrome photographed as a gym. Both said: we are done with the 1980s. Bathrooms went silver overnight. Kitchens followed. Furniture followed the kitchens because the same buyers walked both aisles.

Oil-rubbed bronze took the 2000s. A dark, almost black-brown finish with bronze showing on the edges, or supposed to. A lot of it was a baked coating on zinc, with the “wear” printed on. The finish matched the Tuscan wall, the dark espresso stain, the wrought-iron chandelier. It was Mediterranean without the boat fare. Builders put it on entire subdivisions. For a while you could not buy a towel ring in anything else at the national chains.

Brushed gold — champagne, “golden champagne,” the names multiplied — arrived as the polite 2010s correction. Not the yellow brass of 1987. A quieter, pinker, more Instagram metal. It went on faucets first, then on cabinet pulls, then on the light fixtures that had been nickel last season. Design accounts treated it as warmth. It was warmth you could SKU.

Matte black had a hard run from about 2015 to 2022. Hex knobs. Long bars. Black on white shaker. Black on walnut-look. Black on everything that wanted to look “modern farmhouse” or “industrial” without choosing. The finish hid fingerprints less well than the ads claimed, showed grease in a kitchen, and turned every room into the same room. When everyone has the same black bar pull, the pull stops being a choice and becomes a default. Defaults date faster than choices.

Then unlacquered brass came back. Living finish. The spots, the darkening, the argument that you should touch your hardware and let it record the touching. This is the old brass without the 1980s lacquer, sold as honesty. Some of it is honesty: solid brass that will take a polish or take a tarnish, your call. Some of it is a coating that imitates tarnish and then chips to a white metal. The word unlacquered is doing a lot of work. Ask what the knob is made of before you ask what year it is pretending to be.

Photo cue: FFF-39b — A 1980s oak cabinet door with original polished-brass knobs beside the same door (or a matching door) re-pulled in matte black, then in unlacquered brass. Rights: a shop or homeowner sequence; no staged “before/after” that implies a fake renovation story.

Knobs are the cheapest way to re-date a cabinet. They are also the cheapest way to fake a renovation in a listing. Swap the oil-rubbed bronze orbs for black bars, paint the oak white, keep the box. The box is still a 1994 box. The hinges may still be the original overlay. A buyer who looks at the jewelry and not the carcass pays for a year that is only skin. A buyer who opens the door and looks at the hinge plate, the shelf pins, the side material — particle, plywood, hardwood — is buying a cabinet.

Zinc is the quiet material in this story. Most “brass” knobs at the big-box price are zinc alloy, plated. Most “oil-rubbed bronze” orbs are zinc. Most matte-black bars are zinc with a powder coat. Zinc casts well, machines cheaply, and takes a finish like a mannequin takes paint. It is not a sin. It is a category. The category fails when the plating wears at the finger point and the white-gray metal shows through, or when last year’s finish is so specific — that orb, that hex, that champagne — that the wear pattern is a timestamp.

What ages: simple unplated metal, or solid brass that can be polished, or a steel pull with a shape so dull it never had a year. A plain round brass knob from 1910 and a plain round brass knob from 2010 are cousins. You can shine them or let them go dark. They do not announce a cable-show season. What dates: the zinc orb in last year’s finish. The oversized hex. The cup pull that was specified to match a faucet that has already been replaced. The complete matching set of twenty-four pulls in a finish that had a three-year run.

Furniture hardware follows the same clock at a slight delay. Dresser knobs went from brass to pewter to oil-rubbed to black to “antique brass” again. A good case piece can wear three generations of pulls and still be the same dresser. That is one reason hardwood case goods outlast the metal cycle. You unscrew the year and put on a quieter one. Bradley Brand Furniture, Warren, Arkansas, builds in hardwood and states a no-particleboard rule in company copy, with a 1902 lumber date. [CITE NEEDED.] A solid drawer front will take a new hole if you must, or hide an old one. A foil-wrapped particle drawer front will not forgive a second drill.

I have pulled oil-rubbed bronze off a decent maple cabinet and found the 1990s satin nickel holes already there, filled with wood putty the color of chewing gum. Under the nickel, a single brass hole, off-center. The door was a calendar. Three owners had bought a new year for six dollars a knob and left the maple alone, which was the right instinct in the wrong order. Change the metal if the metal bothers you. Do not mistake the change for a kitchen.

The hangover is in the drawer I started with, and in the donation bin: bags of perfectly good pulls in a finish nobody will admit to wanting for another fifteen years. Brass will come back. It has. Black will come back after people get tired of the living finish they just installed. Nickel is already waiting. The cycle is not a secret. The industry prints it in the fixture catalogs a year before it hits the furniture floor.

Furniture pulls run a half-step behind the kitchen, which is useful if you watch the fixture aisle. When the faucet goes champagne, the dresser follows in a season. When the faucet goes black, the nightstand does too. A bedroom that matched a 2017 kitchen in matte black will look like a 2017 kitchen even after the kitchen has gone back to brass. That is how a house gets out of phase with itself: each room updated to a different metal year, none of them talking. The quietest fix is to pick one dull, refinishable metal and let the loud rooms wait.

If you want a knob that will not scold you in 2030, buy a simple shape in a metal you can refinish, or a metal that was never finished in the fashionable sense. If you want this year’s kitchen in an afternoon, buy the orb. Know which purchase you are making. One is hardware. The other is a subscription to the year, billed in bags you will not throw away.

item.title: The Top That Dates the Kitchen
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
You can date a kitchen without opening a cabinet. Stand at the sink and look down. Harvest-gold tile with a dark grout line, 1970s, maybe into the early 1980s if the owner was loyal. A laminate with a gold fleck or a woodgrain that never fooled anyone, still doing the job. A matte solid-surface in “cameo white,” the color of a dentist’s tray. A granite with a bullnose thick as a wrist, speckled like a parking garage, 2004. A quartz with a printed marble vein that repeats every eight feet if you know where to look. A true marble with etching around the lemon plate. A butcher-block island with a blackened knife scar. The backsplash lies. The top tells the truth.

Formica is a company, not a generic. Formica Corporation grew out of a 1913 material — a laminate originally meant as an electrical insulator, a substitute for mica, which is the joke inside the name. [CITE NEEDED on the exact founding story and the Westinghouse connection as usually told; do not print a founder anecdote without a page.] By midcentury the company had put a wipe-clean sheet on American tables and counters. Diners, kitchens, school desks. The pattern names are a history of what people wanted to pretend: wood, stone, a solid color that would not chip the way paint chips. Laminate is still a decent answer when it is a sheet over a decent core and you are honest that it is a sheet. It became a punchline when the granite boom needed a loser.

Photo cue: FFF-40a — A sequence of kitchen tops: 1970s tile, midcentury Formica, Corian, 2000s granite bullnose, quartz “marble,” a thick hardwood butcher block. Rights: original photography in houses or a salvage yard; label each decade.

DuPont introduced Corian in the late 1960s. [CITE NEEDED on the precise commercial year — 1967 is the date often repeated.] A solid surface: acrylic and mineral, renewable in the sense that a burn or a stain could be sanded, the sink joined to the deck in one pour if the fabricator knew the glue. For a while Corian was the quiet luxury, the hospital and the custom bath, the kitchen that did not want grout. Then it became the builder upgrade, then the thing granite replaced, then the thing people are quietly hiring again because they are tired of stone theater. A material that can be sanded has a second life. That fact keeps returning, whatever the showroom is selling.

Granite had a boom that people still date, loosely, from the late 1990s through about 2010. New houses, flipped houses, the refinanced kitchen. Islands the size of cars. Ogee edges, then bullnoses, then a square edge that was supposed to look “modern.” The stone was real. The fashion was the polish, the thickness, the particular Uba Tuba and Baltic Brown and “salt and pepper” that every slab yard had in stacks. Granite said: we are not laminate. We have arrived. The arrival was heavy. The resale script required it. A kitchen without granite, for a decade, was a kitchen that had not tried.

Quartz — the engineered stone, crushed mineral in a resin — came up as granite’s cleaner cousin. Caesarstone, founded in Israel in 1987, is the name the industry uses for the category’s early commercial life. [CITE NEEDED on the 1987 date and the first export year; mark it until a company or trade-page is in hand.] Other brands followed. The pitch was consistent: the look of stone, fewer pits, less sealing, a color that could be specified like paint. Then the pitch became marble. Not marble. A pattern of marble, printed or veined through the slab, repeating, available in a dozen whites. Instagram did the rest. A kitchen could be Carrara without Carrara’s etching, without Carrara’s price, without Carrara. The vein that repeats is the tell. Once you see the repeat you cannot unsee it.

Marble itself — the real calcite, the soft one — had the Instagram years as a backdrop and a pastry counter. Beautiful, high-maintenance, honest about lemon juice. People bought it because the photograph was the kitchen they wanted. People regretted it because a kitchen is not a photograph. Etching is not a failure of character. It is the material. If you want the photograph to stay, you bought the wrong stone, or you bought the quartz that imitates the photograph.

Photo cue: FFF-40b — Close detail: a repeating quartz “marble” vein at a seam, versus a marble with etching, versus butcher block with a planed repair. Rights: original macro shots.

Tile counters belong to an older, more repairable idea. A cracked tile is a tile. Grout is a maintenance schedule. 1970s tile is loud in color and often better in spirit than the granite that replaced it: you can change a square. You cannot change a bullnose slab without a crew and a dumpster. I have seen tile tops from 1974 that were ugly and sound. I have seen granite from 2006 that was fashionable and already a renovation problem because the next owner “doesn’t do granite.” The stone did not change. The script did.

Butcher block is the return that looks like a grandmother and a restaurant at once. Maple, sometimes oak, sometimes walnut if the budget was proud. A thick hardwood top can be planed. Knife marks, scorch, the gray of raw onion — you take a sixteenth off and you have a new top, the same top. That is the older contract between a kitchen and a tree. Bradley Brand Furniture, Warren, Arkansas, is a hardwood shop, not a counter fabricator; its own copy still states the useful rule: hardwood, no particleboard, a lumber line it dates to 1902. [CITE NEEDED — company copy.] Soft contrast, not a sales pitch: a thick hardwood block can lose a bad year with a plane. A printed quartz pattern cannot. The pattern is the slab. Sand the fashion off a print and you have a duller print, or a resin you were not supposed to see.

What dates a kitchen is almost always the top, because the top is the surface you photograph and the surface you sell. Cabinets can be painted. Hardware can be swapped. The slab is a decision you live with at every meal. A 2004 granite island with a fat ogee is a calendar even if the cabinets have been painted twice. A 2019 quartz marble-vein with waterfall ends is already picking up the tone of a finished fad in some zip codes. Give it five more years of rentals and it will be “the quartz kitchen,” said the way people now say “the Corian kitchen.”

What ages is a top with a repair path. Real marble, if you accept the etch. Corian, if you accept the look. Tile, if you can stand grout. Butcher block, if you oil it and stop treating it like a photograph. Solid hardwood, period. Laminate, honestly, if the core is sound and you are not pretending it is stone. The enemy is not a material. The enemy is a material sold as a permanent arrival. Granite was sold that way. Quartz is being sold that way. Nothing at elbow height is a permanent arrival. It is a work surface. Work leaves marks.

The hangover is in the slab yards and the landfill. Granite remnants too specific to reuse. Quartz colors that had a catalog year. Tile that was demolished because a realtor said stone. Formica that was ripped out while it was still wiping clean. A lot of perfectly serviceable tops died to satisfy a listing. That is fashion with a contractor attached.

The 1970s tile kitchen that still works does so because someone recaulked and replaced a square. The Formica kitchen that still works does so because someone did not put a slow cooker on a dry burn and then decided the house needed stone. The granite kitchen that still works does so because the owners stopped caring whether granite was “over.” Caring is the expensive part. Materials are cheaper than the feeling that your elbow is out of fashion.

If you are choosing a top now, ask the sanding question. Can this lose a stain, a burn, a year? If the answer is no, you are buying a picture. Pictures are allowed. They are not counters in the older sense. The older sense is a thickness you can afford to waste a little of, every decade, and still cook.

item.title: Sleeping in the Lobby
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The bed was a white field. Two giant Euro shams sat up like headstones, a row of smaller pillows in front of them in a graded march, a throw folded at the foot with a care that no one who has to catch a train would repeat on a Wednesday. A bench at the end of the bed held a tray that held nothing. Blackout drapes. A lamp that was a sculpture. The alarm clock, if it existed, had been hidden. You were at home. You were also, unmistakably, in a hotel that had been flattened into a floor plan.

Ian Schrager, coming out of Studio 54 and into hotels, hired Philippe Starck in the late 1980s and 1990s to make the lobby an event and the room a mood. The Royalton in New York (1988) is the usual first chapter. [CITE NEEDED on the exact opening month and on which interiors were Starck’s end to end.] The Paramount, the Delano in Miami Beach (1995), the Mondrian in Los Angeles — the list is the one hotel histories recite. Starck put a dwarfing chair in a lobby, a ghostly Louis somewhere it did not belong, a bathroom that performed as a nightclub. The bedroom, in the American imagination that followed, became white, spare, a little theatrical, and flattering to a body that had just been in a lobby.

Photo cue: FFF-41a — A 1990s Starck/Schrager hotel bedroom or lobby (Royalton, Delano, or Mondrian), archival or licensed publicity. Rights: hotel or photographer archive; do not scrape a guest’s phone photo and call it documentary.

What America took home was not the lobby chair. Most living rooms cannot absorb a Starck scale. What came home was the bed. White duvet. Hotel-weight linens, or the catalog version of hotel-weight. Euro shams — those 26-by-26 (or larger) squares that sit against the headboard and make a pillow army. A bench at the foot, as if a valet might set a suitcase there. A low dresser that was more minibar than heirloom. The bedside table cleared of everything except a book you were not reading. Home as a place you check into.

The older American bedroom had been a private clutter: a wedding suite of dark wood, a quilt, a television, a pile of clothes on a chair that had given up being a chair. The boutique hotel said that privacy could look public. Your bedroom could have the same discipline as a corridor you admired. That discipline is a staff. Turndown is a job. The white duvet is easy to photograph and hard to keep if you drink coffee in bed. People bought the photograph and then hired the laundry they could afford, which was themselves, on a Sunday.

Restoration Hardware — later RH — spent the 2010s turning that stay into a catalog and then into actual hotels. The company had already sold the Belgian linen, the huge bed, the iron canopy, the gray-and-white palette that photographed as money. RH Hotels made the loop explicit: sleep in the store. [CITE NEEDED on the first RH hotel opening date if you print the city and year as a lead fact.] You could stay in the mood, then buy the bench. Hospitality and retail have always borrowed from each other. This was less borrowing than a merger of the floor and the folio.

Photo cue: FFF-41b — A domestic bedroom styled as a boutique hotel: white duvet, Euro shams, bench at the foot, blackout drapes, one orchid. Rights: original interior; caption it as a home, not a hotel, so the comparison stays honest.

Status, here, is traveled. Not necessarily traveled. The look of having been in a better hotel than the Marriott your in-laws book. The white bed said European even when the sheets were a domestic brand with a thread-count number that is mostly a marketing argument. [CITE NEEDED before repeating any specific thread-count claim as if it were a standard.] The bench said you had enough floor that a piece of furniture could do nothing all day. The empty nightstand said you were not the kind of person who needed a glass of water, a bottle of pills, and a paperback with a broken spine. Most people are that kind of person. The room punished them for it.

Hospitality-grade is a real specification. Contract textiles, mattresses built for a turn every few months, drapery that can take a blackout liner and a housekeeping cart. A hotel bed is engineered for abuse and for speed: strip, replace, repeat. Sheets are a size that fits a cart. Duvet covers close with a method a night staff can do in the dark. The catalog mood is the opposite engineering. It is a look that assumes you will not actually live like a guest. A guest does not own the room. A guest does not store tax documents in the bench. When a home copies a hotel without the spec, you get a white duvet that pills, a bench that collects mail, and Euro shams that spend six days on a chair because nobody has time to rebuild the pillow wall.

The bench at the foot is the tell. In a hotel it is a luggage stand with manners: a place for a bag, a tray, a morning coffee that will not find a table. In a house it is often a leftover from the catalog page, upholstered in a fabric that will take the first pair of shoes as an insult. A hardwood bench with a simple seat can do the hotel job and the house job. An upholstered ottoman-as-bench in the exact gray of the headboard is only doing the page. I have sat on both. The wood one had a pile of books. The gray one had a dry-cleaning bag and a look of apology.

I have slept in rooms that got the spec right — a tight sheet, a duvet that could be washed, a headboard that did not collect dust in tufting — and in rooms that got only the mood. The mood rooms are the ones in the design feeds. They look like rest. They require labor. Rest and labor are not the same purchase. The boutique hotel hid the labor behind a wage. The catalog hid the labor behind a photograph of a couple who had just arrived.

What ages in this fashion is the simple part of the kit, if the materials were honest. A decent hardwood bench can lose the tray and the suitcase act and become a place to put shoes. A solid headboard can be recovered. White linen, if it is linen, can go gray in a way that is not ugly. What dates is the full performance: the pillow march, the orchid, the bench that matches the nightstands that match the dresser that matches a lobby in 1995 or a catalog in 2016. The performance is a stay. Stays end.

Bradley Brand Furniture, Warren, Arkansas, does not sell a hotel. Company copy talks about hardwood, a refusal of particleboard, a lumber date of 1902. [CITE NEEDED.] A case piece from a shop like that can sit in a bedroom that is not performing hospitality and still make sense: a dresser that holds the pills and the paperback. The quiet contrast is use. A hotel room is emptied every morning. A bedroom is not. Furniture that assumes the empty morning will look wrong by Thursday.

The hangover is a generation of bedrooms that feel slightly ceremonial. People apologize for the mess as if a night manager were arriving. Teenagers inherit the Euro sham and throw it on the floor. The white duvet goes off-white and then gets replaced with a darker quilt, which is how bedrooms return to being bedrooms. The bench stays, because a bench is useful, and then it grows a pile. The pile is the truth. Let it.

Schrager and Starck changed what a public room could feel like. That is a real achievement in hotels. The mistake was believing a public feeling was a private requirement. You do not have to sleep in a lobby. You can sleep in a room that has a glass of water on the table and a chair that is allowed to hold a shirt. If you want the white field, buy one pillow you will actually use and a cover you can wash on a weeknight. Leave the rest of the army at the front desk.

The boutique bedroom taught Americans to want a better bed. Good. Then it taught them that the bed should look unused. That second lesson is fashion. Fashion can be stripped in the morning, like a guest leaving, and the frame can stay.

item.title: The Chair Was Fine. The Fabric Was a Year.
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
The chair had a decent bone. You could feel it when you lifted one corner: a hardwood rail, a sprung seat, weight that was not all foam. Over the bone, a cream bouclé the color of a labradoodle. The loops had gone gray on the arms and shiny on the headrest. A single thread had pulled near the seam and started a run that no one would stop, because stopping it meant admitting the chair was already last year’s cloud. The frame could have taken another cloth. The cloth was the purchase people remembered.

Bouclé is not a 2020 invention. The word is French for buckled or looped; the cloth is a yarn with knots and loops that photograph as texture. Eileen Gray used it. So did the wider midcentury trade: the woolly, nubby upholstery on a club chair or a Bibendum that needed to read as modern without reading as slick. Le Corbusier, Pierre Jeanneret, and Charlotte Perriand’s Grand Confort has spent much of its later life in a pale bouclé that people now treat as original law. [CITE NEEDED on which early production fabrics were actually specified; later showrooms have a habit of backdating a cream loop.] The old bouclé was wool, or wool-enough, and it sat on frames that were the point. You bought the chair. The cloth was a coat.

Then 2020 through 2023 made the coat the chair. Every direct-to-consumer brand, and a few old ones that wanted the traffic, issued a cream blob: a rounded lounge, a “cloud,” a sheepish kidney of foam and wood-look legs, all in the same off-white loop. The silhouette was midcentury if you squinted and nursery if you did not. The cloth hid a lot of cheap foam. Texture is camouflage. On a feed, at three feet, the chair looked expensive and soft. In a room, on a July afternoon, it looked like a pet.

Photo cue: FFF-42a — An Eileen Gray Bibendum or a documented midcentury bouclé chair beside a 2021 cream blob lounge from a DTC catalog. Rights: museum or licensed archival for the Gray; original or brand-licensed for the contemporary piece, captioned as a type.

Velvet ran a parallel, older cycle. Crushed velvet in the 1990s — the sofa that looked wet, the jewel tones, the swirl that changed when you sat. It was prom and a casino and a suburban basement. People fled it for microfiber, then for the linen-look slipcover, then for velvet again. The 2020s version arrived as “performance velvet”: a polyester pile with a stain-resistant finish, sometimes a Crypton or Crypton-type treatment, sometimes an indoor-outdoor weave that had left the patio. Sunbrella, long a name for a deck chair that would not rot, came inside and sat on a sofa that would never see rain. The selling point was the child, the dog, the red wine. The effect was a velvet that did not behave like velvet. It behaved like a uniform.

Crypton and the other performance weaves are a real chemistry. I am not mocking a parent who wants a sofa that can take a spill. I am naming the fashion. Once “performance” became the default swatch, a whole run of sofas photographed as the same matte pile in the same ten colors. Navy. Emerald. Camel. The jewel tones of the 1990s without the crush. The cloth announced that you were a practical person with a design account. That announcement dates. Practical people will still need a washable sofa in 2032. They will not need this particular pile in this particular emerald.

Photo cue: FFF-42b — Three arm details: 1990s crushed velvet, 2020s performance velvet, a wool bouclé with a pulled loop. Rights: original macro photography; no brand logos required.

Fabric is the fastest date stamp on a good frame because fabric is the cheapest thing to change in a factory photograph and the first thing a room sees. A frame — hardwood rails, proper joinery, a spring unit that can be re-tied — is slow money. A mill can change a SKU of cloth in a season. Retail follows the mill. You sit down in a showroom and think you are choosing a chair. You are choosing a year, in a fiber.

The cream bouclé year was cruel to pale loops. Dirt is not a moral failure. Dirt is physics. A looped yarn holds a crumb. A cream loop displays it. People covered the chairs with throws, which defeated the blob, or they lived with a gray that crept inward from the arms like a tide. Resale listings filled with “barely used” cream chairs that were used the ordinary amount. The next fashion will be a darker bouclé, or a velvet, or a leather-look that photographs as “quiet.” The frames, if they were frames, will still be there.

Recover versus replace is the only adult question. If the bone is good — hardwood, a spring deck, corners that do not rack — recovering is the older economy. You pay a shop. You pick a cloth that is not this year’s blob. You get the chair back as a chair. If the bone is foam on a plywood silhouette with legs that unscrew from inserts, recovering is a donation to a shape that was never meant to outlast the cloth. Replace that one, or live with it until the lease ends. Do not send it to an upholsterer and pretend you bought a Gray.

Bradley Brand Furniture, Warren, Arkansas, is a hardwood house. Company copy: lumber lineage dated 1902, no particleboard. [CITE NEEDED.] They are not an upholstery mill. The contrast still holds. A solid case piece does not wear a date in a looped yarn. A chair with a real frame can change its date. A blob with a costume cannot. Buy the frame if you can find it. Buy the cloth knowing you will argue with it.

I have sat in a 1960s lounge with new wool and felt the original decision in the angle of the back. I have sat in a 2021 cream loop and felt only foam finding its sitting-shape. Both were called bouclé in the caption. The caption is a swatch name. It is not a provenance. Eileen Gray does not owe the blob anything. The blob owes Gray a footnote and a more honest hangtag.

What ages: a frame you can recover; a wool or a tight-weave linen that wears into itself; a leather that was leather. What dates: the cream loop of 2021, the crushed swirl of 1996, the performance emerald that matched a thousand rooms, the indoor-outdoor stripe that still looks like it is waiting for a deck. One pillow in a fashion cloth is a note. A whole sofa in a fashion cloth is the song.

The hangover is already at the curb on bulk-trash mornings: blob chairs that cannot stand a second cloth, velvets that went bald at the headrest, slipcovers in a bouclé-look knit that stretched. A few of those pieces had frames. Most did not. The ones that did will be recut. The ones that did not will become the next decade’s joke, the way crushed velvet became a joke and then a nostalgia and then a joke again.

Indoor-outdoor cloth coming off the patio is the latest version of an old wish: that a sitting room could take weather. Weather, indoors, is a child, a dog, a belt buckle, a Saturday. Sunbrella and its cousins will take some of that. They will also take the room toward a pool house, even if the pool is a hope. If that is the room you want, fine. If you wanted a club chair and got a deck chair in a nicer color, look at the selvage. The mill told you. The hangtag used the word performance the way a catalog used lifestyle. Both words mean: this cloth is the product. The chair is the delivery device.

If you like the loop, use it on something whose bones you have checked. If you like velvet, ask whether you want the crush, the performance, or the old cotton pile that marks when you sit. Marks are not the enemy. A mark means a person was in the room. The enemy is a cloth that cannot take a mark and cannot take a new cloth. That is a costume with legs.

Sunbrella can stay outside. It can also come in, if you want a sofa that behaves like a patio. Just do not call that hospitality, or midcentury, or a cloud. Call it a cover. Covers come off. That was always the point of a good chair.
